weeks.title: Every Member Has a Gift
weeks.keyText: As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.
weeks.theme: A gift is not my trophy but something the Lord has entrusted to me for serving the body.
group: Read 1 Peter 4:10-11. What does the title “good managers” remind you of?
Have you ever felt that you “have no gift”? What have others seen in you?
Tell one another one gift you see in each other—how can you encourage each other to use it this week?
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, notice the many unseen kinds of service during the gathering: sound, ushering, cleaning, children’s ministry, preparing refreshments. Before the service, pray for these co-workers; afterward, find one of them and say thank you. And ask the Lord to show you: in this body, where can I put my hands to work?

lessons.title: Good Managers of God’s Grace
lessons.hear:
Over these past weeks we have moved from life to relationships: learning to be members of the body, to love one another, to handle conflict, and to forgive one another. Now we enter another stage—ministry. The order of the 321 Vision is life first, then relationships, then ministry. Ministry without life is a machine spinning its wheels; ministry without relationships easily hurts people. But where there is life and there are relationships, ministry grows naturally, like fruit. No wonder that before Peter talks about gifts, he first says, “Above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves” (1 Peter 4:8).

Peter goes on: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms” (1 Peter 4:10). This sentence holds three important truths.

First, “each”: every Christian has received a gift, without exception. New believers, older believers, introverts, those with limited mobility—all are included. The Holy Spirit does not place a member into the body without giving it a function.

Second, “has received”: a gift is received, not earned. In the New Testament, the word for “gift” comes from the same root as the word for “grace”; it means something freely given. So those who have gifts have no reason to be proud, because the gift isn’t their own achievement; and those who haven’t yet discovered their gifts have no reason to feel inferior, because the gift doesn’t depend on your qualifications.

Third, “good managers”: a manager is not the owner. The owner entrusts his household to a manager so that he will run it well, for the good of the whole household. Gifts are not for building my reputation; they are for serving one another. Peter also states the purpose of serving: “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11). Today, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes to see the gifts he has placed in you.
lessons.light: To let Jesus receive all the glory is one of the two core commitments of the 321 Vision. Once a gift is treated as “mine,” it becomes a stage for pride; when it is treated as “entrusted by the Lord,” it becomes a vessel for service. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: ministry is the natural overflow of life and relationships.
think: In 1 Peter 4:8-11, which relational practices are mentioned before serving?
Am I more prone to pride because of my gifts, or to feeling inferior because I can’t see any?
How will I ask the Lord to let me see the gifts he has given me?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for freely giving me gifts, even though I don’t yet fully know them. Open my eyes to see what you have placed within me, and make me a faithful, good manager—not for my own name, but to serve others, so that you may be glorified in all things. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today write down three things that bring you joy to do and that have helped others (for example, keeping someone company, organizing things, teaching children, cooking). Pray over the list: “Lord, are these the gifts you have given me?”
lessons.quick: Every member has a gift; I am the manager, not the owner.
text: And above all things be earnest in your love among yourselves, for love covers a multitude of sins.
Be hospitable to one another without grumbling.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.title: Think of Yourself Reasonably
lessons.hear:
A retired brother had sat in church for thirty years without ever serving. When asked why, he said, “I can’t preach and I can’t sing. I don’t have any gifts.” Then one day the church organized visits to the elderly, they were short of helpers, and he was pulled in to lend a hand. That day he spent two hours chatting with an elderly man who lived alone, and the old man held on to his hand and wouldn’t let go. In the car on the way home, his eyes suddenly filled with tears: “So I can do this too.”

Our old mindset often pictures gifts as up-front and visible: preaching, leading worship, leading Bible study. When we see others on the platform, we feel like we’re nothing. But the gifts Paul lists are quite different: prophecy, service, teaching, exhorting, giving, leading, showing mercy (see Romans 12:6-8). Among them, “service” means practical help, “exhorting” means encouraging people, and “showing mercy” means being with those who suffer. These usually happen offstage, yet the body can’t do without them.

Paul also says, “not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.” (Romans 12:3). To “think reasonably” is to see clearly and accurately—neither inflating nor belittling ourselves. The proud see themselves too highly, the insecure see themselves too lowly, and neither sees themselves through God’s eyes.

God’s perspective is this: “so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (Romans 12:5). You don’t need to envy other people’s gifts, and you mustn’t bury your own. That retired brother later became a core member of the church’s eldercare team. He said, “I missed thirty years, but the Lord never gave up on me.”
lessons.light: Pride and inferiority are both self-centered ways of seeing. Humility is returning to my proper place and seeing myself through God’s eyes. Selflessness is not emptiness but entering the limitless: when I stop staring at myself and look only at what the Lord has entrusted to me, I can live out the gifts he has placed within me.
think: Which gifts are listed in Romans 12:3-8, and which of them usually happen “offstage”?
Have I assumed I have no gifts simply because I’m not up front?
What behind-the-scenes service brings me joy when I do it?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, forgive me for measuring gifts by human standards—envying the platform and looking down on the work behind the scenes. Help me see myself through your eyes, to think of myself reasonably, neither proud nor insecure. If I have buried my gifts for a long time, call me afresh today. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today ask a brother or sister who knows you well (your spouse, small group leader, or spiritual companion): “What gift do you think God has placed in me?” Write down their answer and thank the Lord for it.
lessons.quick: Think of yourself reasonably: neither too highly, nor burying your gift.
text: For I say through the grace that was given me, to everyone who is among you, not to think of yourself more highly than you ought to think; but to think reasonably, as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith.
For even as we have many members in one body, and all the members don’t have the same function,
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another,
having gifts differing according to the grace that was given to us: if prophecy, let’s prophesy according to the proportion of our faith;
or service, let’s give ourselves to service; or he who teaches, to his teaching;
or he who exhorts, to his exhorting; he who gives, let him do it with generosity; he who rules, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

lessons.title: Discovering Gifts by Serving
lessons.hear:
When God had the Israelites build the tabernacle, the first person he called by name was not a priest or a prophet, but a craftsman. The LORD said, “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel … I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship” (Exodus 31:2-3).

This passage tells us two things. First, God’s Spirit fills not only those who preach, but also those who cut gemstones and carve wood. Accounting, design, plumbing and electrical work, cooking, writing code—all of it can be offered to God and used to build his dwelling place. Different traditions understand the relationship between spiritual gifts and natural talents differently, but all agree that whatever is set alight by the Holy Spirit and used to build God’s house comes from God. Second, Bezalel didn’t work alone; God appointed Oholiab “with him” (Exodus 31:6). Gifts always flourish in partnership.

So how do you discover your gifts? Often the best way is not to fill out a questionnaire and then wait, but to discover them while serving. You don’t learn to swim standing on the shore, and gifts often become clear only after you get in the water. Here are three simple clues:
1. Joy: when you do this, you feel joy and energy inside, not just reluctant duty.
2. Fruit: others are helped and built up by what you do.
3. Confirmation: mature brothers and sisters around you see it and affirm it too.

Try it once today. Say to your small group leader or a ministry leader, “I’d like to give it a try—is there anything you need help with?” You don’t have to find “the perfect place for me” right away; start with one need. Many people discover what God has put in their hands while they are serving tea, setting out chairs, or looking after children.
lessons.light: The Way of Service begins with “Spirit”: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Bezalel was first filled with the Spirit of God, and only then could he do all kinds of work. Serving from the heart, relying on the Holy Spirit, brings gladness; serving from the head, relying on myself, brings worry. Gifts are set alight in the Holy Spirit and brought to completion in partnership.
think: In Exodus 31:1-6, how did God prepare Bezalel and Oholiab?
Which of my everyday abilities could I offer to God to build his house?
To whom am I willing to say “I’d like to give it a try” this week?
lessons.speak: The LORD God, you called Bezalel by name and filled him with your Spirit. Fill me with your Spirit too, so that my hands and my abilities may be used to build your house. Give me courage to take the first step and to come to know the gifts you have given me as I serve. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today send a message to your small group leader or a ministry leader: “Is there anywhere you could use an extra pair of hands lately? I’d like to give it a try.” Then complete one small act of service this week.
lessons.quick: Gifts often show up only after you get in the water: start with one need.
text: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
“Behold, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
to devise skillful works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in bronze,
and in cutting of stones for setting, and in carving of wood, to work in all kinds of workmanship.

Behold, I myself have appointed with him Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan; and in the heart of all who are wise-hearted I have put wisdom, that they may make all that I have commanded you:

lessons.title: The Talent Buried in the Ground
lessons.hear:
In the parable of the talents, the first two servants put their master’s money to work and both made a profit. But the third servant buried his one talent in the ground. When the master returned, he handed back the money untouched and explained why: “I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth” (Matthew 25:25).

This servant’s problem wasn’t that he did something wrong; it was that he did nothing at all. The root was fear: fear of failure, fear of loss, fear of his master. His picture of his master was distorted too: “Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man” (Matthew 25:24). When we see God as a harsh taskmaster, we would rather do nothing than risk doing something wrong.

Today, review your heart: Have I buried my gifts? There are many ways to bury them. Some people bury them out of fear: “I won’t do it well, and people will laugh at me.” Some out of hurt: “The last time I served I was criticized; I’m not doing that again.” Some out of busyness: “I’ll wait until the kids are older and work is more settled.” Some out of comparison: “She does it better than I do; there’s no place for me.”

There is also an opposite error: treating our gifts as our own stage—willing to serve only where we can be seen, and walking away the moment we aren’t appreciated. That is just as self-centered.

The way to adjust begins with getting to know the master again. Our Lord is not a hard man; he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. He entrusts gifts to us not to catch our mistakes, but because he trusts us and wants us to share his joy. If you set aside serving because you were hurt, first ask the Lord to heal that wound; you might also talk with a pastor you trust. If it is only fear, hand that fear to the Lord, then dig up that talent—even if all you do first is something very small.
lessons.light: Fear of failure is often the other side of the self-centered life: caring so much about our own face that we dare not take a risk. When the focus is on Jesus and not on myself, I am no longer bound by failure. “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)—when it is he who serves through me, I can serve boldly.
think: In Matthew 25:24-29, why did the third servant bury the talent?
Which of these has buried my gift—fear, hurt, busyness, or comparison?
What small act of service can I dig up first today?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I have often buried the gifts you entrusted to me because of fear, hurt, busyness, or comparison. Heal the wounds I have received in serving, and remove my wrong ideas about you. You are the Lord who trusts me, and I am willing to bring my gifts out once again to be used by you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today write down one ministry you once did but later stopped. Honestly write the reason you stopped, then ask the Lord: In what small way could I start again now?
lessons.quick: The Lord is not a harsh taskmaster; dig up the gift you’ve buried.
text: “He also who had received the one talent came and said, ‘Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man, reaping where you didn’t sow, and gathering where you didn’t scatter.
I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the earth. Behold, you have what is yours.’
“But his lord answered him, ‘You wicked and slothful servant. You knew that I reap where I didn’t sow, and gather where I didn’t scatter.
You ought therefore to have deposited my money with the bankers, and at my coming I should have received back my own with interest.
Take away therefore the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents.
For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.

lessons.title: Stir Up the Gift Like a Flame
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote to young Timothy to remind him: “I remind you that you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:6-7).

A gift is like a bed of coals. Left alone, it slowly gathers ash and may even go out; stirred often and fed with fuel, it burns brighter and brighter. Timothy’s gift was kindled through Paul’s laying on of hands, within a relationship of spiritual father and son; and his faith had been passed down from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (see 2 Timothy 1:5). Gifts never grow in a vacuum; they are discovered, stirred up, and passed on within relationships.

This week we have seen that every member of the body has a gift; that gifts are freely received and must be managed well; that gifts often become clear through serving; and that fear buries gifts, while trust stirs them up. Now, pass this on to one person.

There are two ways to multiply. First, be someone’s “reminder.” You may see a person’s gift before they see it themselves. A simple “I think you’re really good at comforting people” or “You’re so patient with kids” may be the very match that lights their service. Second, be someone’s “co-worker.” Invite a newcomer or a younger believer to serve alongside you, the way Paul took Timothy along, teaching as you go. Paul said, “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2).

The ministry of the church is not held up by a few people; it is many stirred-up members burning together. Today, you can be the one who stirs the fire.
lessons.light: The 235 relationships of spiritual parents and children are the very channel through which gifts are passed on: Paul stirred up Timothy, and Timothy in turn entrusted others who were faithful. When changing our mindset reaches multiplication, ministry is no longer one person’s heavy burden but a body of members each doing their part, building God’s system together.
think: In 2 Timothy 1:5-7, how were Timothy’s faith and gift passed on to him?
What new understanding of my own gift have I gained this week?
In whom can I “stir the fire,” or whom can I invite to serve with me?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for placing gifts in me and in every member of the body. Take away my spirit of fear and give me a spirit of power, love, and self-control, so that I stir up my gift like a flame. Make me one who stirs the fire too, who sees and encourages the gifts in others, so that your house is built up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today tell a brother or sister one specific gift you see in them, and invite them to join you in an act of service this month.
lessons.quick: A gift is like a bed of coals: stir it up and pass it on.
text: having been reminded of the sincere faith that is in you, which lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and, I am persuaded, in you also.
For this cause, I remind you that you should stir up the gift of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands.
For God didn’t give us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.

weeks.title: The Five-Fold Ministry: Equipping the Saints
weeks.keyText: for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ,
weeks.theme: The ascended Christ gave ministries to the church not so that a few would do the work, but to equip every saint to do their part.
group: Read Ephesians 4:11-13. What is the shared purpose of the five ministries? Which phrase moves you most?
In your experience, has church felt more like “a few perform while most watch,” or like “everyone doing their part”? Why?
Which co-worker or leader will you tell this week, “Thank you for equipping me”? What is one thing you will do?
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, before you walk into church, tell the Lord, “Lord, I’m not here to watch others serve today—I’m here to be equipped.” During the service, notice the people at the pulpit and at every post, and ask which ministry function each one is carrying. Afterward, ask yourself: what is the Lord equipping me to do? Then pray for one co-worker.

lessons.title: Gifts From the Ascended Christ
lessons.hear:
Ephesians 4 paints a triumphant scene: Christ has conquered death and ascended on high, like a victorious king returning to his city and handing out the spoils to his people. Paul begins, “But to each one of us, the grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ” (Ephesians 4:7). Then he names the most remarkable gift the ascended Lord gave his church—not a pile of resources, not a system, but people: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers” (Ephesians 4:11).

We can understand these five ministries by their function. Apostolic ministry pioneers, lays foundations, and sends. Prophetic ministry listens for God’s heart and awakens the church to its direction. Evangelists carry the good news beyond the church walls. Shepherds care for the flock and walk alongside the weak. Teachers explain the truth and set firm foundations. Whether the offices of “apostle” and “prophet” continue today is understood differently in different traditions: some see them as foundation-laying offices for the church (see Ephesians 2:20) that have completed their work; others believe they continue. But however we understand that, the church today still cannot do without any of these five functions—pioneering, revealing direction, proclaiming, shepherding, and teaching.

The most important verse is verse 12: “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12). The root of the word translated “perfecting” is the same word the Gospels use for fishermen “mending” their nets (see Matthew 4:21)—repairing what is torn and untangling what is knotted so the net can go back out to sea. The purpose of these ministries is not for leaders to do the work in place of the saints, but to mend and equip the saints so that every one of them can cast the net.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes: the Lord gave these ministries for you.
lessons.light: Self-centered service wants to be needed, so it keeps the work in its own hands. Selfless service finds its joy in equipping others and gladly lets them grow beyond itself. None of the five ministries is a throne; each is a servant’s post. To let Jesus reign is to let every ministry submit to Christ the Head, so that together we build up his body.
think: In Ephesians 4:7-13, what are the purpose and the goal of the ministries Christ gave?
Do I see service as “the pastor’s job,” and myself merely as someone to be served?
In what area am I willing to be equipped this week so that I can do my part?
lessons.speak: Ascended Lord Jesus, thank you for giving apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds, and teachers to your church. I confess that I often want only to be fed, not to be equipped. Mend the torn nets of my life, equip me to do my part, and let your body be built up through me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the five ministry functions. Next to each one, write the name of someone who has helped you in that way, and pray one sentence for each of them.
lessons.quick: Ministries don’t do the work for the saints; they equip the saints to do their part.
text: But to each one of us, the grace was given according to the measure of the gift of Christ.
Therefore he says, “When he ascended on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts to people.”
Now this, “He ascended”, what is it but that he also first descended into the lower parts of the earth?
He who descended is the one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things.
He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers;
for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ,
until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,

lessons.title: Are All Apostles?
lessons.hear:
For ten years, one church’s pastor did nearly everything himself: preaching, visiting, counseling, leading worship, fixing the air conditioning, driving the elderly to church. The members would say, “Our pastor can do anything.” Then he collapsed from exhaustion and was hospitalized—and the church discovered that no one else could lead a Bible study, and no one else knew which families needed a visit. In the hospital corridor, one of the elders said quietly, “We treated him as if he were the church, and we were just the audience.”

Behind this lies a very common old mindset: ministry is for the “professionals,” and since we give our offerings, we have the right to be served. But God sees it completely differently. Paul first says, “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually” (1 Corinthians 12:27). Then he asks a string of questions: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers?” (1 Corinthians 12:29). The answer is obviously no. No single person has every ministry—not even the most gifted pastor.

These words break down two ideas at once. One is “the pastor should be able to do everything”—which puts a person in a place only Christ can occupy. The other is “I’m nothing”—which forgets that I, too, am a member of the body. God distributes different ministries to different people precisely so that we will need one another: pioneers need shepherds to follow up, shepherds need teachers to put down roots, and teachers need evangelists to bring people in.

When we see it this way, we stop treating our pastors as superheroes and stop treating ourselves as outsiders. The five-fold ministry is like the different positions on a soccer team. The coach doesn’t go onto the field and play in the players’ place; he trains every player well and sends them onto the field.
lessons.light: Treating a pastor as a superhero puts a person in God’s place; treating myself as a spectator leaves my proper place as a member of the body. Both are self-centered. Humility means returning to our proper place: letting God be God, letting the pastor be a pastor, and letting me be a member who is equipped and who serves. Changing our mindset means moving from “they serve me” to “together we build up the body of Christ.”
think: In 1 Corinthians 12:28-30, why does Paul keep asking, “Are all…?”
Do my expectations of my pastor treat him as someone who can do everything?
What is one task, now carried only by the pastor or a few co-workers, that I could share?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, forgive me for pushing all the service onto the pastor and a few co-workers while I simply sit back to criticize or enjoy. Forgive me, too, for sometimes treating people as superheroes and forgetting that only you are almighty. Show me my place in the body, and make me willing both to be equipped and to give myself. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask your small group leader or a co-worker, “Is there something you’ve been carrying alone lately that I could help with?” Listen, then take on one small part of it.
lessons.quick: No one has every ministry; we need one another to be one body.
text: Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.
God has set some in the assembly: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracle workers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, and various kinds of languages.
Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all miracle workers?
Do all have gifts of healings? Do all speak with various languages? Do all interpret?
But earnestly desire the best gifts. Moreover, I show a most excellent way to you.

lessons.title: The Ministry Team at Antioch
lessons.hear:
The church at Antioch is a beautiful picture of a team: “Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul” (Acts 13:1). These five men came from very different backgrounds: a Levite, a man probably from Africa, one raised in a royal court, and a former persecutor of the church. Their gifts differed and their origins differed, yet they were united in one thing—“As they served the Lord and fasted,” the Holy Spirit spoke.

Notice that this team first served the Lord together and only then were sent out. Prophetic listening and the rooting work of teaching led to apostolic sending and evangelistic going. The five functions did not compete with one another; they worked together. Later, Barnabas and Saul went out to pioneer, while those who stayed kept shepherding and teaching. Those who went and those who stayed shared one mission.

Today’s practice has two steps. First, recognize which ministry function tends to flow out of you most. When you see a new need, do you want to start something (pioneering)? Do you often sense direction as you pray (listening)? Do you naturally want to tell people about Jesus (proclaiming)? Do you care about who didn’t show up and who is struggling (shepherding)? Or do you love making the truth clear (teaching)? Second, don’t look only at yourself—affirm others. Today, find a brother or sister whose function is different from yours and tell them specifically, “This way you serve has equipped me.”

When we see and affirm one another, a church slowly changes from a crowd of people each busy with their own thing into a team like Antioch—serving with one heart and sent out by the Holy Spirit.
lessons.light: The “5” in 235 is about becoming comrades-in-arms on a five-fold ministry team. Self-centered people compare themselves with others’ gifts and grow jealous; selfless people rejoice when they see others’ gifts, because those gifts are the richness of Christ’s body. Affirming others is one of the simplest ways to let Jesus receive all the glory. People matter more than tasks; a sincere word of affirmation often strengthens co-workers more than an entire event.
think: In Acts 13:1-3, under what circumstances did the Holy Spirit speak?
Of the five ministry functions, which one flows out of me most? Which one am I most lacking?
Which brother or sister with a function different from mine will I affirm?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, thank you for bringing different people together at Antioch into one team serving with one heart. Help me recognize the ministry function you have placed in me, and help me appreciate the gifts in my brothers and sisters that are different from mine. Lead me today to speak one word that builds someone up. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to a brother or sister whose gifts differ from yours. Tell them specifically which time their service helped you, and let them know you will pray for their ministry.
lessons.quick: The five ministries don’t compete; they serve with one heart and equip one another.
text: Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.

lessons.title: Are You Jealous for My Sake?
lessons.hear:
Moses was worn out from leading the people, so God took the Spirit that was on Moses and shared it with seventy elders so they could carry the burden with him. But two of the elders, Eldad and Medad, had not gone out to the Tent—yet the Spirit rested on them too, and they prophesied in the camp. Young Joshua was alarmed: “My lord Moses, forbid them!”

Joshua’s motive looked loyal—he wanted to protect Moses’ authority and keep order. But Moses saw what lay underneath: “Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!” (Numbers 11:29). Moses was not afraid of others having gifts, and not afraid of sharing his position. His only longing was that God’s people would all be used by God. That is a selfless leader.

In the church, Joshua-style reactions are not rare. A newcomer turns out to be great at leading worship, and a long-time co-worker feels a twinge of resentment. Another small group grows, and we say, “They’re just noisy.” Someone proposes a new ministry direction, and our first thought is, “Who does he think he is?” We think we are guarding the church, but really we are guarding our own position. Sometimes we even raise one kind of ministry above the rest: “Evangelism is what’s truly spiritual,” “Teaching is what has depth,” “Shepherding is what shows love”—and that, too, is a hidden form of comparison.

Today, review your heart honestly: when someone else’s gift is noticed, is my heart glad or sour? The way to adjust is to learn Moses’ prayer: “Lord, put your Spirit on him too; use him even more.” When you can sincerely pray for someone else’s ministry to be blessed, you have moved from Joshua toward Moses.
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power; jealousy is refusing to let go of the power of “only I can.” Selflessness doesn’t mean having no gifts—it means no longer putting myself at the center. Humility breeds humility: a leader willing to share the stage will raise up co-workers willing to equip others, while pride provokes pride, and everyone loses.
think: In Numbers 11:26-29, how did Joshua and Moses react differently to the same event?
Whose gifts have been noticed recently in a way that made me uncomfortable inside?
How can I sincerely bless that brother or sister’s ministry?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that when others are used by you and noticed by everyone, comparison and jealousy often rise in my heart. I tell myself I’m guarding the church, when really I’m guarding my own position. Give me a heart as large as Moses’ heart, longing for all your people to be used by you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Think of a co-worker you have quietly compared yourself with or resented. Today, pray three times for their ministry, asking God to use them even more; if it’s appropriate, give them a sincere word of blessing in person.
lessons.quick: May all the Lord’s people be used—including the one who makes me jealous.
text: Moses went out, and told the people the LORD’s words; and he gathered seventy men of the elders of the people, and set them around the Tent.
The LORD came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was on him, and put it on the seventy elders. When the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied, but they did so no more.

But two men remained in the camp. The name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad; and the Spirit rested on them. They were of those who were written, but had not gone out to the Tent; and they prophesied in the camp.
A young man ran, and told Moses, and said, “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp!”
Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his chosen men, answered, “My lord Moses, forbid them!”
Moses said to him, “Are you jealous for my sake? I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets, that the LORD would put his Spirit on them!”

lessons.title: Explaining God’s Way More Accurately
lessons.hear:
Apollos was a richly gifted preacher: “an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man … He was mighty in the Scriptures” (Acts 18:24). He was fervent in spirit and preached boldly in the synagogue. But his understanding was incomplete—he knew only the baptism of John. Then a lay couple who made tents, Priscilla and Aquila, heard him. They didn’t criticize him in front of the congregation. Instead, “they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately” (Acts 18:26).

This is one of the most beautiful scenes of equipping the saints. Priscilla and Aquila were not apostles, and they had no pulpit, yet in their own home they carried out the functions of teaching and shepherding. The equipped Apollos later went on to Achaia, where “he greatly helped those who had believed through grace.” Paul planted, Apollos watered—and behind them was a couple quietly equipping others. That is how equipping is passed on, generation after generation.

This week we have seen that the ascended Christ gave the five-fold ministry to equip the saints; that no one has every ministry, so we need one another; that we serve with one heart as a team; and that we must overcome jealousy and be glad when others are used. Now comes the final step, multiplication: take what you have been equipped with and equip someone else.

You don’t have to wait until you are a “minister” to begin. Maybe it’s reading a chapter of a Gospel with a new believer. Maybe it’s taking a young person who has just started serving out for a meal, listening to their struggles, and sharing the road you have walked. Like Priscilla and Aquila, with gentleness and patience, help make God’s word a little clearer. That is how the church grows, little by little, “to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13).
lessons.light: The last step in changing a mindset is multiplication. Those who have been equipped go on to equip others; this is the relationship of spiritual parents and children in 235. The focus is not on how many gifts I have, but on whether Jesus, through me, helps someone else grow and serve too. Truth that stops with me grows stagnant; passed on, it brings life.
think: In Acts 18:24-28, how did Priscilla and Aquila help Apollos?
How has my view of “whose job ministry is” changed this week?
Which younger or newer brother or sister will I equip?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for equipping me through so many people. Make me like Priscilla and Aquila—not criticizing others in public, but explaining your way more accurately in love. Today, lay on my heart one person who needs to be equipped. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, invite a new believer or someone just beginning to serve for coffee or a thirty-minute video call. Listen to their faith and their service, share a passage that has helped you, and pray for them.
lessons.quick: When the equipped go on to equip others, the church grows generation after generation.
text: Now a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by race, an eloquent man, came to Ephesus. He was mighty in the Scriptures.
This man had been instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, although he knew only the baptism of John.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. But when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside, and explained to him the way of God more accurately.
When he had determined to pass over into Achaia, the brothers encouraged him; and wrote to the disciples to receive him. When he had come, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace;
for he powerfully refuted the Jews, publicly showing by the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ.

weeks.title: The Way of Service: Spirit · Insight · Life · Serve · God
weeks.keyText: I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
weeks.theme: Service doesn’t begin with our hands but with remaining in the Lord: relying on the Spirit, gaining insight from the Word, living out his life, serving under his reign, and giving glory to God.
group: Read John 15:4-5. What does “apart from me you can do nothing” say to you about your service?
Of the five words—Spirit, Insight, Life, Serve, God—which is weakest for you right now? What recently happened that showed you this?
How could our small group practice one of these words together this week? Have each person share one concrete way we can remind one another.
weeks.sunday: The night before Sunday, bring each of your church responsibilities before the Lord one by one and tell him, “Apart from you, I can do nothing.” During the service, ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on your motives in serving. Afterward, whether or not you were up front today, say a word of thanks to God and give the glory to him.

lessons.title: Spirit: Remaining in the Vine
lessons.hear:
On the night he was betrayed, Jesus gave his disciples a very simple picture: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch never has to grit its teeth and “try hard” to bear fruit. It only has to stay connected to the vine; the sap flows in, and the fruit grows naturally.

This is the starting point of all service. The 321 Way of Service has five words: Spirit, Insight, Life, Serve, God. This week we will walk one word each day, and the first word is “Spirit”—the Holy Spirit is my guide. Jesus promised, “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). Concretely, remaining in the Lord means letting the Holy Spirit lead before, during, and after every act of service—rather than letting experience, habit, or other people’s expectations lead.

In the Old Testament, Zerubbabel led a weary people in rebuilding the temple, with few resources and much opposition. God told him, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit” (Zechariah 4:6). The church today often falls into the same temptation: thinking that if we have enough people, enough budget, and a well-designed program, the ministry will succeed. All of these are useful, but none of them is the sap.

A pianist can play every note correctly, and a small group leader can run the meeting smoothly, while inside they have been dry for a long time. A branch cut from the vine may stay green for a day or two, but it no longer has life. Today, before your service begins, stop and ask, “Holy Spirit, how do you want me to do this?”
lessons.light: Lean on the Holy Spirit with your heart, not on yourself with your head; serve from the heart and you’ll find joy, serve from the head and you’ll find worry. Weariness in ministry often comes not from doing too much, but from doing it while cut off from the vine. The first step in letting Jesus reign is handing control back to the Holy Spirit before we serve, letting him decide what to do, how to do it, and where to stop.
think: In John 15:1-8, how many times does the word “remain” appear? What is the condition for bearing fruit?
Is my recent service being guided by the Holy Spirit, or pushed along by habit and pressure?
Before I serve next time, how will I first quiet myself and seek the Holy Spirit?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the vine and I am a branch. I confess that I often serve by my own experience and strength, and even apart from you I think I’m doing fine. Holy Spirit, guide me afresh today. Let your life flow into me, so that my service comes from you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, before your next act of service (preparing a lesson, rehearsing music, replying to group members), be still for three minutes, read John 15:5, and ask the Holy Spirit, “How do you want me to do this?” Write down one sentence you receive.
lessons.quick: Cut off from the vine, even the busiest service bears no fruit.
text: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer.
Every branch in me that doesn’t bear fruit, he takes away. Every branch that bears fruit, he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.
You are already pruned clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.
Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.
I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
If a man doesn’t remain in me, he is thrown out as a branch and is withered; and they gather them, throw them into the fire, and they are burned.
If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you will ask whatever you desire, and it will be done for you.
“In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.

lessons.title: Insight: One Thing Is Needed
lessons.hear:
One sister who oversaw her church’s fellowship meals got up at five every Sunday morning to cook, washed dishes in the kitchen during the service, and kept cleaning up until the afternoon. One day she couldn’t help telling her small group leader, “I’ve served in this church for eight years, but I can’t remember the last time I quietly read the Bible.” There was no complaint in her voice—only an emptiness she couldn’t put into words.

Martha was like that too. She welcomed Jesus into her home because she truly loved him; but “Martha was distracted with much serving,” and in the end she blamed even the Lord: “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone?” Jesus answered gently, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed” (Luke 10:41-42).

Our old mindset often says that doing more is how we love the Lord, and sitting down to listen is laziness. But Jesus’ view is that the source of service is listening to his word. This is the second word on the Way of Service, “Insight”—grasping and obeying the truth of Scripture. The Bible is my standard: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). Service that hasn’t first gained insight at the Lord’s feet easily turns into frenzy, comparison, and even bitterness.

But “Insight” isn’t only hearing; it includes doing. James reminds us, “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22). Mary’s sitting down was not an escape from service but the way to better service. Later she anointed Jesus’ feet with very costly ointment (see John 12:3)—service that came only after she had gained insight at his feet.

Today you don’t have to drop all your service, but you do need to return first to the Lord’s feet.
lessons.light: Self-centered service easily slides into “I do more than you” comparison, and even into blaming the Lord. Selfless service first receives at the Lord’s feet and then acts according to his word. When our perspective shifts from “what I do for the Lord” to “being with the Lord,” service turns from frenzy into joy. The Bible is my standard, not my tool.
think: In Luke 10:38-42, what does Jesus say Martha is “anxious and troubled” about?
In my service, am I more like distracted Martha or like Mary sitting and listening?
How will I set aside time this week to “sit at the Lord’s feet” before I serve?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that I am often anxious and troubled about many things, using busyness to prove I love you while rarely sitting at your feet to hear you speak. Help me choose the good part—to gain insight into truth from your word, and then to serve according to it. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, take fifteen minutes out of your preparation time for tomorrow’s service. First read a passage related to that service, then write down one insight and one concrete way you will obey it.
lessons.quick: Sit first at the Lord’s feet, then stand at your post of service.
text: As they went on their way, he entered into a certain village, and a certain woman named Martha received him into her house.
She had a sister called Mary, who also sat at Jesus’ feet and heard his word.
But Martha was distracted with much serving, and she came up to him, and said, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister left me to serve alone? Ask her therefore to help me.”
Jesus answered her, “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,
but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.”

lessons.title: Life: By the Grace of God
lessons.hear:
Paul was one of the most fruitful servants of the early church, yet when he looked back on his life, his first words were not “Look how much I’ve done,” but “For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9). Then he revealed the secret of all his service: “But by the grace of God I am what I am … yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10).

This is the third word on the Way of Service, “Life”—cultivating and living out the life of Jesus. Jesus is my example. Paul’s labor was not something he forced out by willpower; it flowed naturally from a life transformed by grace. Service is the fruit of life, not a substitute for it. If I am very spiritual in the pulpit but short-tempered at home, very efficient in team meetings but impatient with my group members, then my service has run ahead of my life.

Jesus himself showed us this kind of life. At the Last Supper he bent down and washed his disciples’ feet, then said, “For I have given you an example, that you should also do as I have done to you.” (John 13:15). He never used his authority to make people serve him; he used it to serve people.

Today, live out this life in one small, unseen task. Maybe it’s staying after the meeting to stack chairs and take out the trash. Maybe it’s quietly taking over a chore for a tired co-worker without letting anyone know. Maybe it’s doing something at home for your spouse or children that you don’t usually do. Service doesn’t begin on the stage; it begins the moment you bend down.
lessons.light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. When the life is right, service naturally has a sweet savor; when the life is wrong, the more we serve, the more people we hurt. A selfless life says with Paul, “yet not I.” When I lay down my own credit, the life of Christ flows out of me—first to those closest to me, and then to the church.
think: In 1 Corinthians 15:9-10, how does Paul view his past, his present, and his labor?
Has my service run ahead of my life? In which relationship is this most obvious?
In what small, unseen task can I bend down and serve someone today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, though you existed in the form of God, you bent down to wash your disciples’ feet. Whatever I am today, I am by your grace. Cultivate your life in me, so that my service is not a performance but an overflow of your life. Lead me today to serve someone in secret. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one act of service that no one will see and no one needs to thank you for: tidying up after a meeting, handling a chore for a co-worker, or doing something for your family you don’t usually do.
lessons.quick: Service is the fruit of life, not a substitute for it.
text: and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
For I am the least of the apostles, who is not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the assembly of God.
But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.

lessons.title: Serve: Ministry Where Jesus Reigns
lessons.hear:
In the wilderness, the Israelites complained once again because there was no water. God clearly told Moses to “speak to the rock before their eyes.” But years of accumulated weariness and anger in the wilderness erupted in Moses at that moment: “Hear now, you rebels! Shall we bring water out of this rock for you?” (Numbers 20:10). He raised his rod and struck the rock twice. The water still poured out, and the ministry still “succeeded”—but God said, “Because you didn’t believe in me, to sanctify me in the eyes of the children of Israel … ” (Numbers 20:12).

This is the most dangerous moment in ministry: God’s power is still flowing, but the servant has already taken the throne. “Shall we bring water… for you?”—Moses put himself at the center, doing God’s work his own way and with his own emotions. This is exactly what the fourth word on the Way of Service, “Serve,” deals with: to serve is to let Jesus reign and to minister by his authority and power, not by my authority or my temper.

Acts 6 gives us a contrast. A complaint arose in the church over the distribution of food. The apostles didn’t get angry, and they didn’t take everything on themselves. They said, “It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables” (Acts 6:2). They kept to the proper place the Lord had given them, had the congregation choose men “full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom,” then prayed, laid hands on them, and entrusted the work to them. The result: “The word of God increased” (Acts 6:7).

Today, review honestly: in my service, do I often act as if I’m the one bringing the water? When I’m criticized, do I seek the Lord first, or strike the rock first? Even though Moses failed, God still let him see the promised land from the mountaintop (see Deuteronomy 34:4), and later he stood with the Lord on the Mount of Transfiguration (see Luke 9:30-31). It is never too late to adjust: lay down the rod, return to God, and let the Lord reign again.
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power. The most hidden pride in ministry is doing our own thing in God’s name. Humility means letting go of power and returning to our proper place: letting people be people and letting God be God. Those filled with the Holy Spirit don’t scramble for position, because they know the true King is Jesus; nor do they need to control everything, because the ministry was always the Lord’s.
think: In Numbers 20:10-12 and Acts 6:1-7, how did Moses and the apostles respond differently to complaints?
In my service, in what situations am I most likely to “strike the rock”?
The next time I’m misunderstood or criticized, how will I let Jesus reign first?
lessons.speak: Lord, I confess that in my service I often act as if I’m the one doing it all for others, doing your work with my own temper and methods, even claiming your glory for myself. Forgive me. Help me lay down the rod in my hand and return to a servant’s proper place. Reign in my service. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Recall a recent moment in your service when you got angry or overbearing, and confess it to the Lord today. If you hurt a co-worker or group member, take the initiative to message them or apologize in person, and tell them you are willing to change.
lessons.quick: God’s power still flowing doesn’t mean I haven’t taken the throne.
text: Now in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplying, a complaint arose from the Hellenists against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily service.
The twelve summoned the multitude of the disciples and said, “It is not appropriate for us to forsake the word of God and serve tables.
Therefore, select from among you, brothers, seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business.
But we will continue steadfastly in prayer and in the ministry of the word.”
These words pleased the whole multitude. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch,
whom they set before the apostles. When they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.
The word of God increased and the number of the disciples greatly multiplied in Jerusalem. A great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.

lessons.title: God: Returning to Give Him Glory
lessons.hear:
Ten lepers cried out together, were sent together to show themselves to the priests, and were cleansed together on the way. But the story’s spotlight rests on only one man: “One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice. He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks” (Luke 17:15-16). Jesus asked, “But where are the nine?”

This is the last word on the Way of Service, “God”—giving all glory to God and giving thanks in everything. The more fruitful our service, the more important this step becomes. The nine received their healing and kept on going. We are like them when we finish a conference, wrap up a retreat, or see someone come to faith—we breathe a sigh of relief and start preparing for the next event, but forget to come back to the Lord and say, “You did this.” The psalmist prayed, “Not to us, LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory, for your loving kindness, and for your truth’s sake.” (Psalm 115:1).

This week we have walked five words. Spirit—remaining in the vine and letting the Holy Spirit guide. Insight—sitting at the Lord’s feet, grasping and obeying the truth. Life—living out the life of Jesus by grace. Serve—letting Jesus reign and serving by his authority. God—coming back to the Lord and giving him the glory. These five words are not a course you finish once; they are a road to walk again every time you serve: seek him before, obey him during, and give thanks after.

Multiplication means passing this road on to others. You can agree with a co-worker that after each time you serve, you’ll ask each other, “What happened today that we need to come back and give God glory for?” When a team forms a habit of thanksgiving, pride has a hard time taking root, and joy flows naturally.
lessons.light: Two core commitments: let Jesus reign, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Service begins by letting him reign and ends by giving him the glory; everything in between is his grace. People who give thanks in everything don’t lose themselves in ministry, because their focus is on Jesus—not on themselves, not on others, and not on circumstances.
think: In Luke 17:11-19, what did the man who came back do?
The last time my service bore fruit, did I think first of myself or of God?
Which co-worker will I invite to practice “giving God the glory after serving” with me?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for leading me along the Way of Service this week. I don’t want to be one of the nine who received grace and walked away. I come back to you and give you all the glory. Make Spirit, Insight, Life, Serve, God the rhythm of every act of service, and let me pass it on to my co-workers. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down three recent experiences of grace in your service and thank God for each one. Then share the five words “Spirit · Insight · Life · Serve · God” with a co-worker and agree to remind each other after the next time you serve.
lessons.quick: Seek him before serving, obey him while serving, and give God the glory afterward.
text: As he was on his way to Jerusalem, he was passing along the borders of Samaria and Galilee.
As he entered into a certain village, ten men who were lepers met him, who stood at a distance.
They lifted up their voices, saying, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
When he saw them, he said to them, “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” As they went, they were cleansed.
One of them, when he saw that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice.
He fell on his face at Jesus’ feet, giving him thanks; and he was a Samaritan.
Jesus answered, “Weren’t the ten cleansed? But where are the nine?
Were there none found who returned to give glory to God, except this foreigner?”
Then he said to him, “Get up, and go your way. Your faith has healed you.”

weeks.title: Serving Without Burnout: Resting in the Lord
weeks.keyText: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
weeks.theme: The Lord isn’t looking for servants who burn out, but for servants who take his yoke, walk with him, and rest in him.
group: Read Matthew 11:28-30. How are the “rest” and the “yoke” Jesus speaks of related?
Have you ever felt exhausted in your service or wanted to quit? What kept you going then, or what made you stop?
How can we share the load with one another this week? Have each person name one task they are willing to share or take over for someone else.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, if you are serving, arrive ten minutes early. Don’t rush into busyness; sit down first and tell the Lord, “I hand this burden over to you.” During the service, notice a co-worker who looks tired. Afterward, pray for them, and honestly ask yourself: did I truly rest this week?

lessons.title: Come to Me for Rest
lessons.hear:
Jesus’ invitation is tender: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). He didn’t say, “Go somewhere,” or, “When you finish all this, you can rest.” He said, “Come to me.” True rest is first of all not a vacation but a Person—rest is found in Jesus himself.

Amazingly, Jesus goes on: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29). Taking on a yoke doesn’t sound restful at all. But in the ancient world, a yoke was often shared by two oxen; a young ox would be yoked beside an experienced one and learn to plow by following its pace. Jesus means that rest is not doing nothing; it is no longer working alone—sharing his yoke and walking at his pace. We burn out not usually because we carry the Lord’s yoke, but because we carry yokes we put on ourselves or that others put on us.

Rest was written into God’s creation from the very beginning: “On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done” (Genesis 2:2). Almighty God doesn’t need rest. He rested to give humanity a rhythm: work is good, and stopping is good too. Later, in the Ten Commandments, God commanded, “You shall labor six days, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God” (Exodus 20:9-10).

This week we are learning to serve without burning out. Before we begin, hear Jesus say to you, “Come to me.” You don’t have to do your service well first in order to earn the right to rest.
lessons.light: Self-centered service shoulders the whole burden, thinking nothing will work without me—which is really trying to take God’s place. Selfless service hands the yoke to Jesus and walks with him. Lean on the Holy Spirit with your heart and you’ll find joy; lean on yourself with your head and you’ll find worry. Rest is an expression of faith: I stop because I believe God is still reigning.
think: In Matthew 11:28-30, how does Jesus describe his own heart? What is his yoke like?
Of the burdens on my shoulders right now, which were given by the Lord, and which did I or others add?
How will I concretely “come to Jesus” for rest this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I come to you with my labor and my heavy burdens. I confess that I often carry yokes I’ve put on myself, thinking things won’t get done without me. Teach me to take your yoke and learn from your gentle and lowly heart, and to find rest in you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, draw two columns on a sheet of paper: “The yoke the Lord gave me” and “The yoke I added myself.” Sort your current responsibilities and areas of service into them, and bring the second column to the Lord in prayer.
lessons.quick: Rest isn’t a place; it’s coming to Jesus.
text: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

lessons.title: You Cannot Do It Alone
lessons.hear:
One small group leader led the Bible study every week, prepared the snacks, followed up with every member, handled every message in the group chat, and also taught Sunday school. Whenever someone offered to help, she would say, “It’s fine—it’s faster if I do it.” Three years later, in the middle of a small group meeting, she suddenly burst into tears: “I’m so tired, but I don’t dare stop. If I stop, the group will fall apart.”

Moses was once that kind of leader. The people “stood around Moses from the morning to the evening,” waiting for him to judge their cases. His father-in-law, Jethro, watched and spoke very bluntly: “The thing that you do is not good. You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone” (Exodus 18:17-18). Notice that it wasn’t only Moses who would wear out—the people would too. When one person does everything, he not only exhausts himself but also stalls the whole community.

We often hold an old mindset: “The capable should carry more,” or “Burning out for the Lord is the most beautiful offering.” These sound spiritual, but God’s view is that ministry belongs to a body, not to one person. Jethro’s plan was clear: Moses would focus on representing the people before God and teaching them the statutes, and would choose “able men which fear God: men of truth” to oversee different levels. “So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you” (Exodus 18:22). Sharing the work isn’t laziness; it gives more members the chance to be used by God.

“It’s faster if I do it” is sometimes true. But it often also means: I don’t trust others, I can’t bear to let go, I need to be needed. Behind that hides a self-centeredness that needs the Lord’s healing. Work handed off may not be done as well at first, but the church will grow more co-workers because of it.
lessons.light: “Nothing works without me” sounds responsible, but it is often leaving our proper place and grasping a position that belongs only to God. Humility is returning to our proper place: I am only one member, not the whole body. Sharing the work is also equipping the saints: when we hand work over, we hand our brothers and sisters the opportunity to serve and to grow.
think: In Exodus 18:17-23, what problem did Jethro see? How did he propose dividing the work?
Do I often say, “It’s faster if I do it”? What is the real reason behind it?
Which of my responsibilities could I begin to hand over or share with another brother or sister?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often think everything will collapse without me. I won’t let go, and I don’t really trust others. Heal my heart that wants to be needed and to stay in control. Give me wisdom as clear as Jethro’s, teach me to share the work, and let more members share the load with me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list the areas of service you carry and choose one that can be shared. Invite a brother or sister to do it with you, and take time to teach them rather than simply dumping the work on them.
lessons.quick: Sharing the work isn’t laziness; it lets more members share the load.
text: On the next day, Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from the morning to the evening.

When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he did to the people, he said, “What is this thing that you do for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning to evening?”
Moses said to his father-in-law, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God.
When they have a matter, they come to me, and I judge between a man and his neighbor, and I make them know the statutes of God, and his laws.”
Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “The thing that you do is not good.
You will surely wear away, both you, and this people that is with you; for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to perform it yourself alone.
Listen now to my voice. I will give you counsel, and God be with you. You represent the people before God, and bring the causes to God.
You shall teach them the statutes and the laws, and shall show them the way in which they must walk, and the work that they must do.

Moreover you shall provide out of all the people able men which fear God: men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.

Let them judge the people at all times. It shall be that every great matter they shall bring to you, but every small matter they shall judge themselves. So shall it be easier for you, and they shall share the load with you.
If you will do this thing, and God commands you so, then you will be able to endure, and all these people also will go to their place in peace.”

lessons.title: Come Apart and Rest Awhile
lessons.hear:
The first time the disciples were sent out to preach, cast out demons, and heal the sick, they came back and excitedly told Jesus “all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught.” Jesus didn’t immediately book their next engagement. Instead he said, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” (Mark 6:31). And the text adds a very down-to-earth detail: “For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.”

No time even to eat—that probably describes many ministry team members. Sundays are busy from morning to night; weeknights are filled with meetings and visits; and someone in the group chats is looking for you twenty-four hours a day. Jesus himself kept a rhythm: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there” (Mark 1:35). Even as he had compassion on the crowds, he set aside time alone with the Father for himself and his disciples.

This is what boundaries are. A boundary isn’t a wall to keep people out; it’s like a riverbank that lets the water flow with direction. A river without banks eventually becomes a swamp. Interestingly, just as they were trying to rest, the crowds followed them again—and Jesus still “had compassion on them” (Mark 6:34). So boundaries aren’t coldness. Sometimes love calls us to respond flexibly, but every day can’t be the exception.

Today, draw one concrete boundary. You might choose a fixed weekly time of rest, such as Monday evening or Saturday morning, when you schedule no ministry and don’t answer church messages, but simply spend time with the Lord and your family. Or you might mute your group chats after a certain hour each night and let your co-workers know your rhythm. Finally, tell someone who can hold you to it.
lessons.light: The order of relationships is God first, then ourselves, then other people, then tasks. Boundaries guard this order: they keep tasks from swallowing people and keep service from swallowing our relationship with God. People matter more than tasks—and that includes you and your family. Sacrificing your family for the sake of ministry is not God’s heart. Only by keeping boundaries can we love for the long haul.
think: In Mark 6:30-34, how did Jesus care for both his disciples and the crowds?
In my life, which time of day or week is most often swallowed by service or messages?
What concrete boundary will I set? Whom will I tell?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for inviting me to come apart with you and rest awhile. I confess that I often let service and messages fill every moment, until I lose even my time with you and with my family. Give me the wisdom and courage to draw boundaries, and give me a compassionate heart so that my boundaries never turn into coldness. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, circle one fixed time of rest on your calendar for this week. Tell your family and one co-worker about it, and ask them not to contact you about ministry matters during that time.
lessons.quick: Boundaries are like riverbanks that give the river of service its direction.
text: The apostles gathered themselves together to Jesus, and they told him all things, whatever they had done, and whatever they had taught.
He said to them, “Come away into a deserted place, and rest awhile.” For there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
They went away in the boat to a deserted place by themselves.
They saw them going, and many recognized him and ran there on foot from all the cities. They arrived before them and came together to him.
Jesus came out, saw a great multitude, and he had compassion on them because they were like sheep without a shepherd; and he began to teach them many things.

lessons.title: Elijah Under the Juniper Tree
lessons.hear:
Elijah had just experienced an earth-shaking victory on Mount Carmel: fire fell from heaven, and the people fell on their faces declaring that the LORD is God. Yet a few days later, a single threat sent him running into the wilderness, where he sat under a juniper tree and asked to die: “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.” (1 Kings 19:4). The greatest victories are often followed closely by the deepest valleys.

Look at what burnout looks like: extreme physical exhaustion, emotional highs and lows, seeing yourself as worthless and your situation as utterly dark, and one overpowering thought—“I, even I only, am left” (see 1 Kings 19:10). Many faithful co-workers arrive at this same place today: they lose their joy in serving, feel irritated whenever church comes up, can’t sleep at night, and don’t want to leave the house on Sunday.

How did God treat this exhausted prophet? He didn’t scold him, and he didn’t immediately give him a new assignment. An angel touched him, gave him bread and water, and let him sleep again. Then the angel came a second time: “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you” (1 Kings 19:7). God cared for his body first. Then he met him in a still, small voice, and finally told him: you are not alone—there are still seven thousand—and you are to anoint Elisha to succeed you (see 1 Kings 19:16-18). Restoration includes rest and an encounter with God, and it also includes companions and successors.

Today, review honestly: am I already sitting under the juniper tree? The adjustment can start with very ordinary things: getting a good night’s sleep, eating a proper meal, telling someone you trust how tired you are. If exhaustion and low mood persist for a long time and affect your sleep, appetite, or work, seeking help from a doctor or a professional counselor is wisdom, not a lack of faith. God often cares for his servants through such people too.
lessons.light: “I, even I only, am left” is the most common lie of burnout, and it is a form of self-centeredness: treating the burden of the whole Kingdom as if it were mine alone. Our focus is on Jesus, not on ourselves or our circumstances. God still has seven thousand in his hand, and still has an Elisha; I only need to walk my own stretch of the road faithfully.
think: In 1 Kings 19:4-8, in what concrete ways did God care for Elijah?
Do I see any warning signs of burnout in myself? Which one is most obvious?
What ordinary step will I take this week to begin recovering? Whom will I tell that I’m tired?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you that you didn’t scold Elijah under the juniper tree, but gave him bread and water and let him rest. I confess that I, too, have times when I’m so tired I don’t want to serve anymore. Care for my body and soul, let me hear your still, small voice, and let me know I am not alone. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Tonight, go to bed an hour earlier and put your phone away. Tomorrow, find a spiritual companion you trust, honestly share how weary you’ve been in your service lately, and ask them to pray for you.
lessons.quick: God first fed the weary prophet, then led him onward.
text: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.
Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”
When he saw that, he arose and ran for his life, and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.

But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree. Then he requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.”
He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!”
He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again.
The LORD’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”
He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, God’s Mountain.

lessons.title: Those Who Wait for the LORD Renew Their Strength
lessons.hear:
Isaiah spoke to a people who were exiled, weary, and discouraged. First he turned their eyes to God: “The everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint. He isn’t weary” (Isaiah 40:28). Then he said something honest: “Even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall” (Isaiah 40:30). Even the youngest, most gifted co-workers have limits. Admitting our limits isn’t failure; it is returning to our proper place as human beings.

Then comes the promise: “but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). Waiting isn’t passive idleness; it is shifting our hope from our own strength to God. The psalmist says, “Unless the LORD builds the house, they who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 127:1). The church is built by the Lord; we are simply his co-workers.

This week we have learned four things: come to Jesus and take his yoke; learn to share the work rather than carrying it alone; draw boundaries that guard our time with God and our families; and face burnout honestly, receiving care from God and from the body. These aren’t just personal wellness tips; they should become the culture of the whole church. A healthy church doesn’t measure who is most spiritual by who is most exhausted.

Multiplication means bringing rest to others. There is surely a weary co-worker near you—perhaps the one who arrives first and leaves last every week, perhaps your pastor. This week you could take over one of their responsibilities so they can sit down and simply worship on a Sunday. Or invite them for a meal where you don’t talk about ministry at all—just keep them company. When we look after one another, our service can go the distance.
lessons.light: Humility is returning to our proper place: admitting that I grow weary and letting God be the God who never grows weary. Humility breeds humility: when leaders are willing to model rest and shared work, co-workers dare to admit they are tired. This is a team that rests in the Lord, and it is what God’s system looks like when it runs in health. God’s system isn’t held up by one person; it is held together by all the members joined to the Head.
think: In Isaiah 40:28-31, what contrast is drawn between God and people? What do those who wait for the LORD receive?
How has my view that “busyness equals spirituality” changed this week?
In what concrete way will I help a weary co-worker get some rest?
lessons.speak: Everlasting God, you never faint or grow weary, but I have weaknesses and limits. Thank you for promising that those who wait for you will renew their strength. Make our church a community that looks after one another and knows how to rest, and use me to bring rest to one weary co-worker. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This week, find an especially busy co-worker or pastor. Offer to take over one of their responsibilities, or invite them to a meal where you won’t talk about ministry, and tell them, “Thank you—you need rest too.”
