lessons.quick: Admit your limits, wait on God, share the load—and your service will go the distance.
text: Haven’t you known? Haven’t you heard? The everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, doesn’t faint. He isn’t weary. His understanding is unsearchable.
He gives power to the weak. He increases the strength of him who has no might.
Even the youths faint and get weary, and the young men utterly fall;
but those who wait for the LORD will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.

weeks.title: 920: Bearing Christ’s Life in Every Relationship
weeks.keyText: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.
weeks.theme: Everyone I am in relationship with is one of my “2s”; when I live out the selfless “0,” Christ bears the “9” in those relationships.
group: Read John 15:8-12. How is the “fruit” Jesus speaks of related to loving one another?
Among your “2s,” which relationship tests you most? Which fruit of the Spirit are you most lacking?
This week, have each person in the group choose one “2” and one fruit, name one concrete action, and share how it went at the next meeting.
weeks.sunday: This Sunday, before you walk into church, think: which of my “2s” will I meet today? During the service, ask the Holy Spirit to show you which part of “self” you need to lay down in a particular relationship. Afterward, bear one specific fruit toward a brother or sister you don’t usually interact with—a kind word, a patient listening ear.

lessons.title: Bear Much Fruit for the Father’s Glory
lessons.hear:
A vine exists for one purpose: to bear fruit. Jesus said, “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples” (John 15:8). He then said nothing about the size of a ministry or the number of people at a meeting. Instead, he spoke of love again and again: “This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you” (John 15:12). It turns out that the fruit the Lord cares about most grows in relationships.

The 321 Vision uses three numbers to help us remember this truth: 920. The “2” is every person I am in relationship with—spouse, children, parents, coworkers, small group members, ministry team members, even the person who gives me headaches. Each one is a field God has placed in my life. The “0” is selflessness—no longer living with myself at the center: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20). Selflessness doesn’t mean being nothing; it means letting the infinite Christ live himself out through me. The “9” is the nine-fold fruit of the Spirit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23).

The order of these three numbers matters: with every “2,” we first return to “0,” and only then does the “9” grow. If we bring “self” into a relationship, the fruit we bear is rivalry, coldness, and comparison. When self drops to zero, the life of Christ has room to flow out.

Jesus also spoke a comforting word: “You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:16). Bearing fruit isn’t an achievement we strive for; it flows from the Lord’s choosing and appointing. Since he has appointed us, he will surely provide. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you which “2s” the Lord has placed around you.
lessons.light: 920 is how the 321 Vision is practiced in relationships: God first (remaining in the vine), then ourselves (dropping to the selfless “0”), then other people (every “2”), and only then ministry. Bearing fruit so the Father is glorified is exactly what it means to let Jesus receive all the glory. The fruit isn’t meant to prove me; it is meant to display him.
think: In John 15:8-17, how many times does Jesus mention “love”? How is bearing fruit connected to loving one another?
When I measure whether I am “bearing fruit,” do I look at ministry results or at relationships?
Which three “2s” will I write down today and pray for?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for choosing me and appointing me to bear fruit. I confess that I often think fruit means ministry results, while I overlook the people around me. Help me see that every person in my life is a field you have entrusted to me, and let me bear lasting fruit in your love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the five most important “2s” in your life—family members, coworkers, small group members, or ministry partners—and beside each name write the one fruit you most need to bear toward that person.
lessons.quick: With every 2, return first to 0, and Christ will bear the 9.
text: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.
Even as the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Remain in my love.
If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, even as I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love.
I have spoken these things to you, that my joy may remain in you, and that your joy may be made full.
“This is my commandment, that you love one another, even as I have loved you.
Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.
You are my friends if you do whatever I command you.
No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.

You didn’t choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain; that whatever you will ask of the Father in my name, he may give it to you.
“I command these things to you, that you may love one another.

lessons.title: Fruit Matters More Than Results
lessons.hear:
A very gifted worship leader always led services that moved people deeply, and his team kept growing. But over the years, several musicians quietly left. One of them said, “On stage he’s very spiritual, but at rehearsals he chews people out.” He himself was baffled: “God is clearly using me—so why can’t the team keep people?”

This is a blind spot for many who serve. Our old mindset says that fruit means results—numbers, achievements, responses, applause. But the fruit Paul speaks of is completely different: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22-23). Not one of these nine can be performed on a stage. Every one of them shows up only in relationships—in the rehearsal room, in the team meeting, at the dinner table at home.

Paul also reminds us that gifts and fruit can’t substitute for each other: “If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2). Gifts are presents the Holy Spirit gives; fruit is the life the Holy Spirit grows. God can use someone with an immature life for a season, but that doesn’t mean God approves of how that person treats others.

Notice what Paul says right after the list of fruit: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit. Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another” (Galatians 5:25-26). Conceit—the hunger for empty glory—is exactly the “self” that makes us prize results over fruit. Only when we no longer need results to prove ourselves do we start caring whether the people around us are doing well.
lessons.light: Self-centered people prize results, because results can prove “me.” Selfless people prize fruit, because fruit displays Christ. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; don’t wound the brothers and sisters around you for the sake of ministry results. Life first, then relationships, then ministry—the order can’t be reversed.
think: In Galatians 5:22-26, what does Paul contrast with the fruit of the Spirit?
Have I ever lost patience or kindness with people around me for the sake of ministry results?
On my ministry team, which fruit do I most need to bear?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, I confess that I often value the results of my service while neglecting how I treat people—very spiritual on stage, yet rough in my relationships. Forgive my hunger for empty glory. Grow in me the fruit of love, patience, and gentleness, so that the people around me find comfort through me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, ask a co-worker who serves with you, “Is there anything about serving with me that makes you uncomfortable?” Listen quietly to the end without defending yourself, simply say thank you, and ask the Lord to change you.
lessons.quick: Gifts are the Spirit’s presents; fruit is the Spirit’s life.
text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith,
gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.
Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.
If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.
Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.

lessons.title: Who Is My “2”?
lessons.hear:
An expert in the law asked Jesus, “Who is my neighbor?” He wanted a list, so he would know where his love could stop. Instead, Jesus told a story. A priest and a Levite saw a man beaten half to death, and both “passed by on the other side.” “But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion” (Luke 10:33). Finally Jesus turned the question around: “Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?” (Luke 10:36).

The lawyer asked, “Who qualifies as my neighbor?” Jesus asked, “Are you willing to be a neighbor to others?” That is exactly what the “2” in 920 means: I don’t get to pick who deserves my love; every person the Lord lets me meet and be in relationship with is my “2.” The priest and the Levite may well have been hurrying to serve at the temple, yet they missed the person right in front of them. We often do the same: busy with church ministry, we “pass by on the other side” of the family member, coworker, or group member who needs us.

The Samaritan’s love was very concrete: he came to him, poured on oil and wine, bound up his wounds, set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, paid for his care, and promised to come back. Love isn’t a feeling; it’s a chain of actions. Jesus ended with, “Go and do likewise” (Luke 10:37).

Today’s practice is to choose someone you tend to “pass by on the other side.” Maybe it’s the person at home you have the least patience with; maybe it’s the coworker no one pays attention to; maybe it’s the quiet member of your small group you have never greeted one-on-one. Do something concrete for that person and bear one fruit: an act of kindness, a time of patient listening, a faithful promise kept. Love doesn’t have to be dramatic, but it must “come to” the person.
lessons.light: The “2” in 920 breaks down our boundaries: my 2s aren’t only the people I like or click with. People matter more than tasks; rushing off to serve while passing by someone who is wounded gets things backward. To let Jesus reign is to let him decide whom I am to love today, rather than letting my preferences decide.
think: In Luke 10:30-37, what concrete things did the Samaritan do?
In my life, which “2” do I most often “pass by on the other side”?
What concrete thing will I do for that person today, and what fruit will I bear?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you didn’t pass me by; you came to me, healed me, and carried me. I confess that I often pick the people I want to love and pass by the ones you have placed beside me. Give me the Samaritan’s compassion, and lead me today to come close and love a “2” I usually overlook. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose the family member, coworker, or group member you most often overlook or have the least patience with, and do one concrete thing for them: a meal, a phone call, or a time of listening without interrupting. Pray for them in your heart as well.
lessons.quick: It’s not who deserves to be my 2, but whose neighbor I’m willing to be.
text: Jesus answered, “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who both stripped him and beat him, and departed, leaving him half dead.
By chance a certain priest was going down that way. When he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.
But a certain Samaritan, as he traveled, came where he was. When he saw him, he was moved with compassion,
came to him, and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. He set him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
On the next day, when he departed, he took out two denarii, gave them to the host, and said to him, ‘Take care of him. Whatever you spend beyond that, I will repay you when I return.’
Now which of these three do you think seemed to be a neighbor to him who fell among the robbers?”
He said, “He who showed mercy on him.” Then Jesus said to him, “Go and do likewise.”

lessons.title: Am I in the Place of God?
lessons.hear:
As a young man, Joseph didn’t understand much about the “0.” He told his brothers his dream: “we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and also stood upright; and behold, your sheaves came around, and bowed down to my sheaf” (Genesis 37:7). His brothers responded with fury: “Will you indeed reign over us?” (Genesis 37:8). Self-centered words stirred up self-centered hatred, and the result was a shattered family and thirteen years of suffering for Joseph.

But God didn’t give up on Joseph. In the pit, in a slave’s household, and in prison, God whittled away his “self” bit by bit. Years later, Joseph had become ruler over Egypt, his old dream had truly come to pass, and his brothers fell down before him saying, “Behold, we are your servants.” It was the perfect moment for revenge—yet Joseph wept and said, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God? As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:19-20).

“Am I in the place of God?”—this is the confession of the “0.” Judgment is God’s business, and I won’t seize his place; ultimate meaning is in God’s hands, and I don’t need revenge to prove myself. From that selfless “0” flowed the “9”: “He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them” (Genesis 50:21). Kindness, gentleness, and goodness grew in the hardest of relationships.

Today, review honestly: in which relationship do I want to sit in God’s place? Perhaps I want to judge the person who hurt me; perhaps I want to control the choices of a family member or group member; perhaps I’m secretly waiting for someone to “get what they deserve.” The first step in adjusting is to tell the Lord, “I am not in your place.” Forgiveness doesn’t deny the hurt, and it doesn’t necessarily restore trust right away; but when we hand judgment back to God, our hearts begin to be free, and fruit begins to grow.
lessons.light: Pride is leaving our proper place as human beings and grasping God’s power; Joseph’s “Am I in the place of God?” is a declaration of humbly returning to our proper place. The “0” doesn’t mean being nothing; it means letting God be God. From a youthful “dream of reigning” to an old man’s “Am I in the place of God?”—that is one person’s journey from the self-centered life to the selfless life.
think: Comparing Genesis 37:5-8 with Genesis 50:15-21, how did Joseph’s attitude toward his brothers change?
In which relationship do I want to sit in God’s place, judging or controlling the other person?
How will I hand judgment in that relationship back to God?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that in some relationships I want to take your place—to judge, to control, to get even. Whittle away my self as you did Joseph’s, so that I can say, “Am I in the place of God?” And let your kindness and gentleness flow out of me. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Write down the name of someone you still want to “get even” with or control. Today, read Genesis 50:19-20 before the Lord, hand your judgment of that person over to God, and pray once for their good.
lessons.quick: I am not in God’s place; when self drops to zero, fruit begins to grow.
text: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,

‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to save many people alive, as is happening today.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

lessons.title: Fruit With the Seed Inside
lessons.hear:
On the third day of creation, God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it” (Genesis 1:11). Inside fruit is seed, and inside the seed is the life of the next tree. The fruit God designed was never meant to end with one bite; it was meant to keep multiplying. The life of Christ is the same: when it bears fruit in a relationship, it leaves a seed in the other person’s life.

Paul’s prayer for the church in Philippi is a wonderful 920 prayer: “This I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment” (Philippians 1:9), and that they would be “filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God” (Philippians 1:11). Notice that the fruit comes “through Jesus Christ” and ultimately goes “to the glory and praise of God.” We are neither the source of the fruit nor its owner.

This week we have walked through 920: everyone I am in relationship with is my “2”; in every relationship I first return to the selfless “0”; and I let the Holy Spirit bear the nine-fold fruit, the “9,” so the Father is glorified. We have also seen that fruit matters more than results; that the question isn’t who deserves to be my 2, but whose neighbor I am willing to be; and that Joseph’s “Am I in the place of God?” allows even the hardest relationships to bear kindness.

Multiplication means handing the seed of 920 to someone else. You could draw it on a small card—a “2,” a “0,” and a “9”—and give it to your spiritual companion or a small group member, telling them in which relationship you experienced it this week. When one person learns to bear fruit in relationships, another person tastes the sweetness of Christ and begins to bear fruit too.
lessons.light: The last step in changing a mindset is multiplication. 920 isn’t one person’s self-improvement; it is a life that gets passed on: the fruit I bear leaves seed in someone else. This is how change from the inside out happens: mindset, life, living, relationships—and only then does ministry naturally grow.
think: In Philippians 1:9-11, what does Paul pray for the believers? To whom does the fruit ultimately go?
In which relationship did I experience the change of 920 this week?
With whom will I share 920, and how?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for teaching me 920 this week. Let my love abound more and more in knowledge and all discernment, and fill me with the fruits of righteousness through Jesus Christ. May every fruit I bear carry seed within it, leaving the seed of Christ in other people’s lives, to your glory and praise. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, make a 920 card, write one thing you received this week on it, and give it to your spiritual companion or a small group member. Share in which relationship you experienced “first return to zero, then bear fruit.”
lessons.quick: Fruit carries seed: the fruit I bear leaves seed in someone else.
text: This I pray, that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and all discernment,
so that you may approve the things that are excellent, that you may be sincere and without offense to the day of Christ,
being filled with the fruits of righteousness which are through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.

weeks.title: 235: Companions, Spiritual Parents, Comrades-in-Arms
weeks.keyText: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
weeks.theme: No one can walk the road of faith alone: God gives me companions to hold me up, spiritual parents to raise me, and comrades-in-arms to labor beside me.
group: Read 2 Timothy 2:1-7. What kinds of people does Paul use as pictures? Which one is most like your situation right now?
Among the 2 (companions), the 3 (spiritual parents and children), and the 5 (comrades-in-arms), which relationship are you most lacking? Why?
This week, whom will you invite to be your prayer companion, or which younger believer will you reach out to and walk alongside? Name the person and the time.
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, as you walk into church, ask the Lord to help you notice three people: a companion who could walk with you, an older believer you could learn from, and a younger one you could come alongside. After the service, spend at least ten extra minutes talking with one of them, and when you get home, pray once for each of the three.

lessons.title: A Four-Generation Relay of Faith
lessons.hear:
When Paul wrote 2 Timothy, he was in a Roman prison and knew that the time of his departure had come. In the last letter of his life, what weighed most on this old soldier of the faith was not his reputation or the size of his ministry. It was one thing: had the faith been placed into the hands of the next generation? He wrote, “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2).

Count the generations in that one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. Four generations, like a relay race. The most dangerous part of a relay is not the track but the handoff zone. No matter how fast you run, if the baton drops, the race is lost. The rise and fall of a church is often decided at the moment of the handoff.

Paul then paints three pictures of how to run our leg well: the soldier, the athlete, and the hardworking farmer (2 Timothy 2:3-6). A good soldier is not a lone hero; he fights in formation alongside his comrades. An athlete must compete by the rules and cannot take shortcuts. A farmer must patiently sow and wait for the harvest. These three pictures line up beautifully with what the 321 Vision calls “235”:

2 — spiritual companions: walking with selfless people and holding one another up. 3 — spiritual parents and children: someone raises me, and I raise others. 5 — comrades-in-arms in the five-fold ministry: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers working together (see Ephesians 4:11-12).

All of this starts with Paul’s opening line: “You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 2:1). Not strong in our own zeal, but strong in grace. This web of relationships is not something we weave by our own effort; it grows out of the grace of one and the same Lord. Today, ask the Holy Spirit to show you that you are not only someone who has received the faith—you are also someone entrusted to pass it on.
lessons.light: The self-centered person treats faith as private property and only wants to be fed. The selfless person knows he is one leg of a relay; he receives in order to hand on. 235 is not an org chart—it is a web of relationships in which Jesus reigns: first with God, then built up together with companions, spiritual parents and children, and comrades-in-arms.
think: Who are the four generations in 2 Timothy 2:2, and what does Paul expect each one to do?
Who passed the baton of faith to me, and have I ever thought about whom I will pass it to?
The soldier, the athlete, the farmer—which picture do I most need to learn from right now?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for placing the faith into my hands through so many witnesses. Forgive me for so often treating faith as my own private business—wanting to receive but not to pass it on. Make me strong in your grace, and provide me with companions, spiritual parents, and comrades-in-arms, so that I may faithfully hand on the baton. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, draw your “faith family tree”: write down the people who led you to the Lord or helped you grow, then leave an empty box below and ask the Lord to show you whom you will one day pass the baton to. Pray one sentence for the generation above you and one for the generation below.
lessons.quick: I have received the baton of faith, and I am entrusted to hand it to the next runner.
text: You therefore, my child, be strengthened in the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
You therefore must endure hardship as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No soldier on duty entangles himself in the affairs of life, that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.
Also, if anyone competes in athletics, he isn’t crowned unless he has competed by the rules.
The farmer who labors must be the first to get a share of the crops.
Consider what I say, and may the Lord give you understanding in all things.

lessons.title: Two Are Better Than One
lessons.hear:
A sister had served in her church for twenty years and carried everything: children’s ministry, the choir, the fellowship meals. Everyone said she was spiritual and capable. Then one year her marriage ran into trouble, and for six whole months no one knew, because she never let anyone get close. Later she said, “I served everyone, but I didn’t have a single companion.”

Many Christians carry an old mindset: “What’s between me and God is nobody else’s business.” It sounds spiritual, but it is often a protective shell of pride or hurt. The Teacher uses the plainest life experience to express God’s view: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10).

Notice that this isn’t talking about two perfect people. It is talking about two people who both fall. A spiritual companion is not a hero who is never weak; it is someone willing to reach out a hand when you fall—and willing to let you reach out your hand when he falls. This is what the 321 Vision means by “becoming spiritual companions with selfless people”: no comparing, no jockeying for first place, no hiding—just open and real.

The Teacher concludes, “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12). When there is a third strand between two people—the Lord himself—that relationship gains resilience. So it was with Jonathan and David: “The soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David” (1 Samuel 18:1). A prince did not fight for the throne; instead he helped the one God had chosen. A selfless companion is one of the most precious gifts God gives the church.
lessons.light: Pride says, “I don’t need anyone.” Hurt says, “I don’t dare to need anyone.” Both leave us fighting alone. Humility returns to its proper place—admitting I am someone who falls, and being willing to let others see my weakness. The third strand of companionship is Jesus; when the focus is on him, two people will neither lean on nor control each other.
think: What benefits of companionship does Ecclesiastes 4:9-12 list?
Am I the one who serves everyone but has no companion?
Who might be the companion God has prepared to walk with me in the Lord?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I confess that I often think I can get through everything on my own, and I don’t let others see my weakness. Tear down my pride and my defenses. Provide me with a selfless spiritual companion, and make me someone who reaches out a hand when others fall. May Jesus be the third strand between us. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, contact a fellow believer of the same gender whom you trust, and invite him or her to talk by phone or meet once a week for the next month to share how you’re doing, confess, and pray for each other. Start with one sentence: “I need you to pray for me.”
lessons.quick: Two people who fall, plus the Lord, make a cord that is not quickly broken.
text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

lessons.title: Many Tutors, Few Fathers
lessons.hear:
Paul said something weighty to the church in Corinth: “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News” (1 Corinthians 4:15). A tutor passes on knowledge; a father passes on life. A tutor leaves when class is over; a father cares for a lifetime. Today’s church has no shortage of speakers and courses—there are more sermons online than we could ever listen to—but spiritual parents who are truly willing to walk with someone as they grow up are few.

Spiritual parenthood is not about age; it is about pouring out your life. Paul goes on to call Timothy “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 4:17). Between them there was love, trust, and a passing on of responsibility. In the Old Testament, Elisha followed Elijah, and at the moment his master was taken up he cried out, “My father, my father, the chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” (2 Kings 2:12). He picked up Elijah’s mantle and carried on the prophetic ministry. Spiritual parenting means handing down both life and mission together.

Today’s practice has two sides. The first is “being a child”: find someone more mature in life than you, humbly learn from him or her, and ask that person to pray for you and to speak the truth to you when you need it. The second is “being a parent”: find someone younger than you or newer to the faith—not to manage them but to walk with them. Read the Bible together, share meals, listen to them, and pray for them.

Paul says, “I beg you therefore, be imitators of me” (1 Corinthians 4:16). That is not pride but responsibility: I am willing to let you see how I follow Christ. You don’t have to be perfect to be a spiritual parent. You only need to be honest, loving, and willing to spend time—and to keep bringing people to Jesus rather than to yourself.
lessons.light: The goal of a spiritual parent is not to make children cling to them but to make them more like Jesus. Good parents say, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Keeping the focus on Jesus prevents control. A self-centered spiritual elder wants people to follow him; a selfless spiritual parent wants people to follow Christ.
think: In 1 Corinthians 4:14-17, what words does Paul use to express his heart for the Corinthian believers?
Is there a spiritual elder in my life, or do I only want tutors and not parents?
Which younger believer or new Christian needs someone to walk with them for a while?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for being my Father, and for raising me through spiritual elders. Give me a humble, teachable heart, and also give me the heart of a spiritual parent, willing to spend time with brothers and sisters younger than I am. Keep me from controlling people or making them depend on me; let me simply bring them to Jesus. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Do two things today: send a message thanking a spiritual elder who once helped raise you in the faith, and arrange to share a meal or read a passage of Scripture this week with a new or younger believer—and listen to their story.
lessons.quick: Tutors pass on knowledge; parents pass on life. I want to be raised, and I want to raise others.
text: I don’t write these things to shame you, but to admonish you as my beloved children.
For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News.
I beg you therefore, be imitators of me.
Because of this I have sent Timothy to you, who is my beloved and faithful child in the Lord, who will remind you of my ways which are in Christ, even as I teach everywhere in every assembly.

lessons.title: Comrades Parted, Co-Workers Restored
lessons.hear:
Paul and Barnabas were the finest comrades-in-arms of the early church. When everyone suspected Saul, Barnabas welcomed him, then brought him to Antioch to serve together. The two were sent out together and endured persecution together. But just before their second journey, they clashed over Mark: “Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other” (Acts 15:39).

Scripture doesn’t cover for either of them. Paul valued the mission and felt that someone who had quit halfway couldn’t be relied on. Barnabas valued the person and wanted to give the young man another chance. Both had a point, yet in that moment neither found a way to make room for the other. Comrades are most often wounded not in front of the enemy but by each other.

Today, quietly review three things. First, in my ministry relationships, do I value “my opinion” more than “our relationship”? Second, have I permanently labeled a brother or sister because of one disappointment? Third, is there a broken ministry partnership for which I am still keeping score in my heart?

The good news is that this is not the end of the story. Years later, writing to Timothy from prison, Paul said, “Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service” (2 Timothy 4:11). The young man who had once been turned away became a co-worker Paul relied on in his final years. God did not let one split define their lives.

Adjustment doesn’t necessarily mean immediate reconciliation. Sometimes it takes time, and it takes willingness from both sides; and if there has been harm or abuse of power in the relationship, it is all the more important to seek help from a trustworthy third party. But there is one thing we can do first: hand the judgment over to the Lord, and entrust that person to God’s grace once again.
lessons.light: Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Comrades-in-arms are not people who never clash, but people who, after a clash, are still willing to return to their proper place and let Jesus reign. People matter more than tasks—ministries can be rearranged, but people must never be casually discarded.
think: What did Paul and Barnabas each value, and how does Scripture describe their parting?
In which ministry relationship have I put my own opinion above the relationship?
For which co-worker I once clashed with can I ask the Lord for a fresh start?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you know the disputes and disappointments I have had with co-workers, and the people I still can’t let go of. Shine your light on the self-centeredness in me, so that I do not treat my opinion as the truth. And in your good time, restore broken relationships, so that we may still be comrades-in-arms in your Kingdom. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the name of someone you once clashed with in ministry, and spend three minutes praying blessing over their ministry and family. If the timing is right, send them a sincere word of greeting.
lessons.quick: Parting is not the end; in the Lord, comrades can stand side by side again.
text: After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let’s return now and visit our brothers in every city in which we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are doing.”
Barnabas planned to take John, who was called Mark, with them also.
But Paul didn’t think that it was a good idea to take with them someone who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia, and didn’t go with them to do the work.
Then the contention grew so sharp that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus,
but Paul chose Silas and went out, being commended by the brothers to the grace of God.
He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the assemblies.

lessons.title: Those Who Are Like-Minded
lessons.hear:
This week we have looked at the three kinds of relationships in 235. Today, in Philippians, let’s see how all three come alive at once in a small band of people.

Paul says of Timothy, “As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News” (Philippians 2:22). That is a spiritual parent-and-child relationship—a passing on of life, and also co-workers laboring side by side. Then he speaks of Epaphroditus: “my brother, fellow worker, fellow soldier” (Philippians 2:25). A brother is a companion; a fellow worker and fellow soldier is a comrade-in-arms. In one person, all three relationships can be woven together.

Paul also says something heartbreaking: “For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2:21). That is exactly the dividing line between the self-centered and the selfless life. 235 relationships are not sustained by technique but by a heart that seeks the things of Jesus Christ. If two people both seek their own interests, even the best relationship turns into a transaction. If two people both seek the things of Christ, even an ordinary relationship becomes a force for the Kingdom.

Picture a fishing net: every knot is tied to four strands. If one strand breaks, the net still holds. The more knots, the stronger the net, and the more fish it can catch. The church is a net like that, and you are one of its knots—connected upward to those who raised you, sideways to your companions and comrades, and downward to those you are raising.

Multiplication means adding one more knot to the net. Today, tell someone what you have received this week, and invite them to start building their own 235. That is how the relay of faith is passed on, leg by leg, to the end of the age.
lessons.light: The last step in changing a mindset is multiplication: if the truth stops with me, it stagnates. 920 reminds me that everyone I am connected to is my “2”; 235 gives those relationships direction—walking together, raising up, and working together. Not seeking my own things, but only the things of Jesus Christ—that is selflessness.
think: How does Paul describe Timothy and Epaphroditus in Philippians 2:19-25?
In my relationships, do I more often seek my own things or the things of Jesus Christ?
With whom will I share what I received this week, inviting them to build 235 relationships too?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for showing me this week that you don’t want me to believe alone. Make me someone who is like-minded with others, not seeking my own things but only the things of Jesus Christ. Surround me with companions, spiritual parents and children, and comrades-in-arms, so that together we may pass the Good News on. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, share this week’s 235 diagram with your spiritual companion or small group: each of you write down your companions, spiritual parents, spiritual children, and comrades-in-arms, and pray together over the empty spaces.
lessons.quick: Seek not your own things but the things of Christ; people like that can be truly like-minded.
text: But I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, that I also may be cheered up when I know how you are doing.
For I have no one else like-minded, who will truly care about you.
For they all seek their own, not the things of Jesus Christ.
But you know that he has proved himself. As a child serves a father, so he served with me in furtherance of the Good News.
Therefore I hope to send him at once, as soon as I see how it will go with me.
But I trust in the Lord that I myself also will come shortly.
But I thought it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother, fellow worker, fellow soldier, and your apostle and servant of my need,

weeks.title: The Great Commission: The Church Reaching Out
weeks.keyText: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
weeks.theme: The church is not a destination but a base: those whom the Lord has won must go and make disciples of all nations.
group: Read Matthew 28:18-20. What are the verbs of the Great Commission? Which one does our church do most often, and which one least?
When you hear the word “missions,” what is the first picture that comes to mind? How does this week’s passage change that picture?
For which unreached people group, which missionary, or which unbelieving friend nearby can our small group pray and take action together?
weeks.sunday: This Lord’s Day, before you walk into church, think: “This is my base, not my destination.” During the service, pray for the missionaries and church planters your church has sent out. Afterward, ask a ministry team member, “What outreach ministries does our church have, and how can I get involved?”

lessons.title: Sent with Authority
lessons.hear:
The risen Lord appeared to his disciples on a mountain in Galilee and left them his final command. Before he said “go,” he said, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18). The Great Commission is not built on the church’s ability but on Christ’s authority. We go out not to sell a religion but to announce a Lord who already reigns.

Then comes the heart of the mission: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). In the structure of the original Greek sentence, the main command is “make disciples”; “go,” “baptizing,” and “teaching” all revolve around that center. In other words, the goal of the Great Commission is not merely to get people to make a decision, but for people to become disciples who follow Jesus and are shaped by the Lord for a lifetime.

The seed of this mission was planted long before, in the Old Testament. When God called Abraham, he said, “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). God never chose one man or one nation so that they could keep the blessing to themselves, but so that through them all peoples would be blessed. The church has inherited that calling: we are blessed in order to become a blessing.

Finally, the Lord gives a promise: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). This promise is not for those who sit still, but for those who “go.” When you are willing to step out, you will experience the Lord’s presence more vividly than ever.

Today, ask the Holy Spirit to open your eyes: the church you attend, your small group, your family—each is a base. The Lord wants us not only to gather but also to scatter; not only to be fed but also to go and make disciples.
lessons.light: Letting Jesus reign means not only that he reigns in my heart, but that his Kingdom expands among all nations. Change your perspective: from “the church exists for me” to “the church and I exist for the world”; from counting heads with earthly eyes to seeing disciples with heaven’s eyes.
think: In Matthew 28:18-20, what does Jesus say before he says “go,” and what does he promise at the end?
Do I see coming to faith as a finish line rather than the starting point of being a disciple and making disciples?
Which sphere of my life—family, workplace, neighborhood—is a place the Lord is sending me?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the Lord who holds all authority in heaven and on earth. Forgive me for only wanting to be fed at church and forgetting that you send me out. Help me see myself as one who is sent, and in your authority and presence, let me make disciples for you, so that all the families of the earth may be blessed through you. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, write down the names of three people in your life who don’t yet know the Lord. Stick the list on your phone or desk, and for the next week pray one sentence for each of them every day, asking the Lord to open a door.
lessons.quick: The Lord has all authority, so I can go; the Lord is always with me, so I need not fear to go.
text: Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.
Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.

lessons.title: From Jerusalem to the Ends of the Earth
lessons.hear:
Just before the Lord ascended, the disciples asked a very “inward-looking” question: “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1:6). They were concerned about the restoration of their own nation and their own place in it. The Lord didn’t rebuke them, but he turned their gaze from inward to outward: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth” (Acts 1:8).

There was once a thriving church. Every Sunday the pews were full, and one program followed another. One year someone proposed sending a couple to plant a church in a country town, but the leadership team hesitated: “We don’t even have enough people for ourselves—how can we send anyone out?” A few years later the congregation was slowly aging, and young people were drifting away one by one. One of the elders later lamented, “We kept guarding the city and forgot that the Lord wanted us to go out of it.”

We often carry an old mindset: “Missions is for missionaries; evangelism is for people with the gift.” But the Lord said “you”—every person who receives the Holy Spirit. Jerusalem is your home and your church; Judea is the culture you know well; Samaria is the people you don’t like, with whom there is a wall between you; the ends of the earth are the far places you have never even considered. These four circles are not levels you complete one after another; they are concentric circles that open up all at once.

The prophet Isaiah long ago spoke God’s heart: “I will also give you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). God has never been satisfied with revival in a small circle. When a church cares only about its own success, it is like a person who only breathes in and never breathes out. Reaching outward is what healthy breathing looks like.
lessons.light: A self-centered church asks, “Will we lose people?” A selfless church asks, “Whom does God want us to send?” Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone (see John 12:24). Denying ourselves—for Jesus, for others, not for ourselves—is not only a personal discipline but also a discipline for a whole church.
think: How does the focus of the question in Acts 1:6 differ from the answer in Acts 1:8?
Who is my “Samaria”? Is there a group of people I deliberately avoid?
In which of the four circles can I take one small step of witness this week?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, come upon me, so that I may receive power to be a witness for Jesus. Forgive me for caring only about myself and the success of my own church, and forgetting that your heart is for all nations. Widen my vision, from my own home to the people I avoid, and all the way to the ends of the earth, so that I may see your salvation everywhere. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify your “Samaria”—a neighbor, coworker, or person from a community you usually keep your distance from. Pray for that person, and this week take the initiative to say a friendly word or do one small kindness.
lessons.quick: A church’s healthy breathing: breathe in grace, breathe out witness.
text: Therefore, when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, are you now restoring the kingdom to Israel?”
He said to them, “It isn’t for you to know times or seasons which the Father has set within his own authority.

lessons.title: A Church Sparked by Nameless Believers
lessons.hear:
How did the church in Antioch begin? Not with a large evangelistic rally led by the apostles, but with a group of nameless believers scattered by persecution. Scripture simply says, “But there were some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, who, when they had come to Antioch, spoke to the Hellenists, preaching the Lord Jesus” (Acts 11:20). We don’t know their names, but they did something very bold for their time: they crossed a cultural boundary and shared the Good News with “outsiders”—Greek-speaking Gentiles. The result: “The hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord” (Acts 11:21).

Then Jerusalem sent Barnabas to have a look. Barnabas, “when he had come, and had seen the grace of God, was glad” (Acts 11:23). He didn’t nitpick about whether this new church was orthodox enough; instead he encouraged them, then went to Tarsus to find Saul, and the two of them taught the disciples in Antioch for a whole year. A work begun by nameless believers, carried forward by Barnabas, who was gifted at coming alongside people, and then by Saul, who was gifted at teaching, became the base that later sent out missionaries.

This is exactly the path of disciple multiplication: someone opens their mouth to share, someone follows up and walks alongside, someone teaches systematically. You don’t have to do it all, but you can be one link in the chain.

Today’s practice is very concrete. From the list of unbelievers you wrote down, choose one and invite them for coffee or a meal. You don’t have to open with a gospel presentation. First, genuinely care about their life and listen to their story; if the opportunity comes, simply share how Jesus has changed you. Also, if there is a new believer near you, go see them like Barnabas did—encourage them and introduce them to people who can help them grow. The fire of the gospel is often lit by just such an ordinary meal.
lessons.light: The Great Commission is not the work of a few stars but of many nameless members working together. Barnabas was selfless: seeing fruit in someone else’s work made him glad, and he went looking for Saul so that someone else could shine. When we let Jesus receive all the glory, we don’t care who sows and who reaps.
think: In Acts 11:19-26, what kinds of people took part in the birth of the church in Antioch?
Of the three links—sharing, walking alongside, and teaching—which do I most often avoid?
Which unbeliever or new believer will I invite for a meal or coffee this week?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for using nameless believers to bring the Good News to Antioch. I am willing to be one link in your hands. Give me courage to open my mouth, and give me Barnabas’s heart, to be glad when I see your grace in others. Prepare the heart of the person I am going to meet. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, send a message to one unbeliever or new believer on your list and set a time this week to share a meal or coffee. Pray for them before you meet, and when you meet, listen more than you talk.
lessons.quick: One sincere meal might spark the beginning of a church.

lessons.title: Jonah Under His Shelter
lessons.hear:
Jonah was the most successful—and most reluctant—missionary in the Old Testament. He preached a single sentence, and the whole city of Nineveh repented. You would think he would be overjoyed. But Scripture tells us he went out of the city and sat in the shade of a shelter “until he might see what would become of the city.” (Jonah 4:5), still hoping that God would rain down fire. It wasn’t that Jonah didn’t understand God’s mercy; it was that he didn’t want God’s mercy to reach people he disliked.

God didn’t give up on Jonah. He taught him using a vine, a worm, and an east wind. When Jonah grew angry because the vine withered, God asked him, “You have been concerned for the vine, for which you have not labored, neither made it grow; which came up in a night and perished in a night. Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also” (Jonah 4:10-11).

Jonah’s problem is often our problem too. We can be very attached to our own “vine”—our comfortable small group, our familiar style of worship, our usual seat, our favorite songs. As soon as newcomers, outsiders, or people from different backgrounds come in and disrupt our rhythm, we feel put out. We may be willing to give money to missions but unwilling to sit next to someone with a different accent.

Today, review honestly: is there a “Nineveh” in my heart—a place I don’t really want God to bless? Am I more concerned about my own comfort than about lost souls?

The book of Jonah ends with a question mark. It never tells us how Jonah finally responded. That question mark is left for every reader. The first step of adjustment is to take that question as God’s word to me today, and to answer him honestly.
lessons.light: The self-centered person treats God’s grace as his own patent, deciding by personal likes and dislikes who deserves salvation; that is leaving our proper place and grasping God’s power. The selfless person returns to their proper place and lets God be God: what God is concerned for, I learn to be concerned for too.
think: In Jonah 4:5-11, what was Jonah concerned for, and what was God concerned for?
Is there a group of people I secretly hope won’t come into our church?
Which “vine” could I let go of so that newcomers can fit in more easily?
lessons.speak: Lord, you are a God of grace and compassion. I confess that I am often like Jonah, more concerned about my own comfort than about people who are lost. Search out the Nineveh in my heart that I don’t want you to bless, and make my heart like yours, loving those you love. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: This Lord’s Day, deliberately leave your usual seat or circle and sit next to a newcomer or someone few people talk to. After the service, spend ten minutes chatting with them and ask how they came to be there.
lessons.quick: The question God asked Jonah, he asks me too: “Shouldn’t I be concerned?”
text: Then Jonah went out of the city and sat on the east side of the city, and there made himself a booth and sat under it in the shade, until he might see what would become of the city.
The LORD God prepared a vine and made it to come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head to deliver him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the vine.
But God prepared a worm at dawn the next day, and it chewed on the vine so that it withered.

When the sun arose, God prepared a sultry east wind; and the sun beat on Jonah’s head, so that he was faint and requested for himself that he might die. He said, “It is better for me to die than to live.”
God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the vine?” He said, “I am right to be angry, even to death.”
The LORD said, “You have been concerned for the vine, for which you have not labored, neither made it grow; which came up in a night and perished in a night.

Shouldn’t I be concerned for Nineveh, that great city, in which are more than one hundred twenty thousand persons who can’t discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also many animals?”

lessons.title: From Being Sent to Sending
lessons.hear:
This week we have traveled from the Great Commission to Antioch. Today we see how this church, begun by nameless believers, became a sending church.

The leaders of the church in Antioch were a remarkable group: Barnabas; Simeon who was called Niger (many scholars believe he came from Africa); Lucius of Cyrene; Manaen, who grew up in the royal court; and Saul, who had once persecuted the church (Acts 13:1). Different ethnicities, different social classes, different backgrounds—yet they served the Lord with one heart. And as they served and fasted, “the Holy Spirit said, ‘Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2).

Think about the cost of that decision. The Holy Spirit did not ask for two peripheral workers but for the church’s two best teachers. The church in Antioch didn’t bargain: “Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away” (Acts 13:3). A healthy church gives its best to God’s Kingdom instead of keeping it for itself.

Disciple multiplication and church planting work much like a family. When children grow up, they leave home and build homes of their own; the parents haven’t lost a child—they have gained another household. A small group that grows can be planted into two; co-workers who mature can be sent; a church that is strong can plant another church. Sending out is not weakening; it is multiplying.

The discipline of multiplication can start today with a very small step: share what you have received this week with a member of your small group, and ask together, “Whom can our small group send out, whom can we walk alongside, and what place can we pray for?” Perhaps you are the one the Holy Spirit is setting apart; perhaps you are the one who prays, lays on hands, gives, and supports. Both are part of the Great Commission.
lessons.light: The last step in changing a mindset is multiplication: a church or a small group that only grows bigger but never sends out will stagnate. When we let Jesus receive all the glory, we don’t measure success by how many people stay with us, but find our joy in how many disciples are sent out.
think: In Acts 13:1-4, in what setting did the church in Antioch hear the Holy Spirit’s voice?
Do my small group and I only want to grow, but not be willing to send people out?
Which missionary or church planter will I pray for and support in a specific way this week?
lessons.speak: Holy Spirit, thank you for using the church in Antioch to send out Barnabas and Saul. Speak in our church and small group, and make us willing to give our best to your Kingdom. If you set me apart, I am willing to go; if you want me to send others, I am willing to pray, walk alongside, and support. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose one missionary or church planter, write them a message of encouragement, and commit to praying for them once a week for the next month. Invite one small group member to do this with you.
lessons.quick: Sending out is not weakening but multiplying; being sent and sending are both the Great Commission.
text: Now in the assembly that was at Antioch there were some prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen the foster brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
As they served the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me, for the work to which I have called them.”
Then, when they had fasted and prayed and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia. From there they sailed to Cyprus.

lessons.title: The Lord’s Prayer: A Kingdom Blueprint
lessons.hear:
We often treat the Lord’s Prayer as something to recite at the end of a service, but what the Lord Jesus gave his disciples was actually a blueprint of the Kingdom. He said, “Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven’” (Matthew 6:9-10).

Notice the order. The first three petitions are all about “your”: your name, your Kingdom, your will. Only the last three are about “us”: our bread, our debts, our temptations. The focus is first on God, then on people. This is the very core of what the 321 Vision calls “build God’s system.” We don’t first build our own plans and then ask God to bless them. Instead, we first let God’s name be kept holy, God’s Kingdom come, and God’s will be done—and then our needs are provided for within his Kingdom.

“May your name be kept holy” is the worship and life of the church: when the world sees believers loving one another and living with honesty and integrity, they honor God’s name. “Let your Kingdom come” means letting Jesus reign in every heart, every home, every small group, and every church. “Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” means bringing heaven’s order into everyday life on earth—leadership decisions, the use of offerings, the handling of conflict—all according to God’s heart.

The prophet Habakkuk saw where this Kingdom is headed: “For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the LORD’s glory, as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14). And the Lord’s Prayer ends with the declaration: “For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen” (Matthew 6:13).

Today, pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly, line by line, and ask the Holy Spirit to show you that this is not just a prayer to recite—it is the lifelong mission of you and your church.
lessons.light: The order of the Lord’s Prayer is the order of the 321 Vision: let Jesus reign, let Jesus receive all the glory, and build God’s system. Self-centered prayer begins with “my needs”; selfless prayer begins with “your name, your Kingdom, your will.” When the focus is on Jesus, the church will have heaven’s order.
think: In Matthew 6:9-13, which lines are about “your” and which are about “us”?
Are my everyday prayers more about “your Kingdom” or about “my business”?
In my small group or ministry, what most needs “let your will be done on earth”?
lessons.speak: Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come in my heart, in my home, and in my church. Forgive me for so often putting my own concerns ahead of your Kingdom. Let your will be done in our relationships and ministry as it is in heaven. Yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, take one minute in the morning, at noon, and in the evening to pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly. After “Let your Kingdom come,” add the name of a small group or ministry you belong to, and ask the Lord to reign there.
lessons.quick: First your name, your Kingdom, your will—then our needs.
text: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
Give us today our daily bread.
Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.
Bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. For yours is the Kingdom, the power, and the glory forever. Amen.’

lessons.title: Glory to the One in the Church
lessons.hear:
At a thanksgiving service celebrating the completion of a new church building, one of the elders gave a speech. From fundraising to design to construction, he thanked every ministry team member who had contributed, and everyone applauded warmly. Afterward, an elderly sister quietly said to him, “Brother, today you thanked everyone—except Jesus.” He couldn’t sleep that night. He knelt down and, with tears, confessed his sin.

We often carry an old mindset: the church is something we built; success is the result of our effort, and failure is someone else’s problem. But in Ephesians, Paul turns all of that upside down with a song of praise: “Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us, to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations forever and ever. Amen” (Ephesians 3:20-21).

Notice three things. First, it is God’s power that accomplishes everything, not our ability—and this power is the power “that works in us.” Second, the glory belongs to him, and it is “in the assembly,” the church. The church is the stage on which God displays his glory, not a stage on which we display ourselves. Third, this glory reaches “to all generations,” outlasting any pastor, any era, any building.

Before this song of praise, Paul first bowed his knees and prayed for the church: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love” (Ephesians 3:17). Letting Jesus reign in the church begins with letting him dwell and reign in each person’s heart. When heart after heart yields the throne to him, the church naturally becomes the place where he is glorified. If you have seen any growth or fruit in your church life this year, remember: it is not your crown but his grace.
lessons.light: Pride grasps God’s power and also steals God’s glory; humility returns to its proper place and lets God be God. The last word on the Way of Service is “God”: give all glory to God and give thanks in everything. When we let Jesus receive all the glory, we can rest in being servants, without carrying the burden of being the master.
think: In Ephesians 3:14-21, what does Paul ask for the church, and to whom does he finally give the glory?
This year, have I without realizing it given the glory for ministry to myself or to some other person?
How can I, in word and deed, give glory to Jesus in the church?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, you are able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that I ask or think, according to the power that works in me. Forgive me for so often stealing your glory and giving the credit to myself or to others. May Christ dwell and reign in my heart, and may our church be the place where you are glorified to all generations. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, list three graces you experienced in church this year, and after each one write, “Glory to Jesus.” Then share one of them in a sentence in your small group chat.
lessons.quick: The church is not our stage; it is the place where he is glorified.
text: For this cause, I bow my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,
from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named,
that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person,
that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love,

Now to him who is able to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that works in us,
to him be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus to all generations, forever and ever. Amen.

lessons.title: Walking with Everyone to Victory
lessons.hear:
Paul’s greatest lifelong desire can be summed up in one sentence: “We proclaim him, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus” (Colossians 1:28). Notice that he says “every man” three times. Paul didn’t only see crowds; he saw each individual. His goal was not a lively meeting but every single person growing mature and victorious in Christ.

This is also the heart of the 321 Vision: to walk with every person until they become an overcomer. Overcomers are not a small spiritual elite; they are ordinary believers who let Jesus reign. The Lord promises, “He who overcomes, I will give to him to sit down with me on my throne, as I also overcame, and sat down with my Father on his throne” (Revelation 3:21). Overcoming doesn’t come from our own straining, but, as Paul says, from “striving according to his working, which works in me mightily” (Colossians 1:29).

Walking with someone until they become an overcomer is like teaching a child to ride a bike. At first you run along holding the back of the seat while they wobble all over the place. Gradually you loosen your grip, but you keep running beside them. Then one day they ride off on their own, turn around, and wave. You don’t have to be a perfect companion; you just have to be willing to run alongside.

Today’s practice is to choose one person you will walk with in the coming year. It might be a spiritual child, a struggling member of your small group, a friend who just came to faith, or a child in your own family. Pray for them, and ask them, “In the new year, in what area do you most want to become more like Jesus? How can I walk with you?” Then set a regular time to read the Bible, pray, and do life together. That way, the Lord’s Prayer is not just on our lips; it is being fulfilled, bit by bit, in a person’s life.
lessons.light: People matter more than tasks: a church’s success is not measured by how many programs it runs, but by how many people are walked with until they become overcomers. 920 reminds me that everyone I am connected to is my “2”; the selfless “0” keeps me from making myself the center and makes me willing to pay a price for someone else’s growth.
think: Paul says “every man” three times in Colossians 1:28. What does that reveal about his heart?
This year, who walked with me, and whom did I walk with?
In the new year, whom will I walk with, and what time will we set?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for walking with me this year through so many brothers and sisters. Give me Paul’s heart to see each individual, and make me willing to strive with your mighty power to walk with people until they are presented perfect in Christ. Show me the one person I am to walk with in the new year. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, choose the person you will walk with in the coming year and send them a message: “In the new year, in what area do you most want to become more like Jesus? I’d love to walk with you.” Then set a time for your first meeting.
lessons.quick: Overcomers are not a select few, but every person who is walked with and lets Jesus reign.

of which I was made a servant according to the stewardship of God which was given me toward you to fulfill the word of God,

We proclaim him, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus;
for which I also labor, striving according to his working, which works in me mightily.

lessons.title: Revival Begins with Humility
lessons.hear:
Many Christians long for a great end-time revival: the gospel spreading far and wide, churches on fire, and the nations turning to the Lord. It is a beautiful hope. Different traditions understand the order of the last days differently, but all believe that God’s Kingdom will fully come. Yet where does Scripture say the doorway to revival lies? When Solomon dedicated the temple, God appeared to him and said, “If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14).

Notice that God says “my people, who are called by my name”—not the world out there, but God’s own people. Revival doesn’t begin with criticizing society; it begins with the church humbling itself. It doesn’t begin with pointing out other people’s problems; it begins with me returning to my proper place.

As the year draws to a close, this is the perfect time for review. Quietly reflect: In my mindset, which human, earthly, temporary perspectives have not yet been turned around? In my life, where do I still insist on being my own lord and king? In my daily living, which habits do I know I should change but keep putting off? In my relationships, is there someone I still refuse to forgive, or to whom I still owe an apology? In my ministry, have I hurt people for the sake of getting things done?

Don’t be afraid to face these questions. James says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Admitting our shortcomings is not failure; it is the doorway to grace. God promises, “I will hear from heaven,” and his eyes and heart are always among his people. The way to adjust is simple: name the specific things, confess them to God, and if needed, apologize to the people involved. Then receive forgiveness and walk into the new year with a lighter heart.
lessons.light: Humility is the key to revival. Pride is leaving our proper place and grasping power; humility—what this verse calls humbling ourselves—is laying down power and returning to our proper place. The great end-time revival will not come through strategy or momentum, but through many selfless people letting Jesus reign. Change begins with me, and so does revival.
think: In 2 Chronicles 7:14, what four things does God ask of his people, and what three things does he promise?
Looking back on this year, which area of the five-fold change most needs my confession and adjustment?
Is there someone I need to apologize to or forgive before the year ends?
lessons.speak: Lord, I am one who is called by your name, and today I am willing to humble myself, pray, and seek your face. Search my mindset, life, living, relationships, and ministry this year, and show me where I still want to be king. I confess my sins to you; give me courage to make things right with others. Hear from heaven and heal our church. In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, take fifteen minutes to write down one thing from this year in each area of the five-fold change that needs confession or adjustment, and pray over them. If one of them involves a brother or sister, apologize or express forgiveness to them before the year ends.
lessons.quick: Revival doesn’t begin with blaming others but with my humble prayer.
text: “If I shut up the sky so that there is no rain, or if I command the locust to devour the land, or if I send pestilence among my people,
if my people who are called by my name will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land.
Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to prayer that is made in this place.
For now I have chosen and made this house holy, that my name may be there forever; and my eyes and my heart will be there perpetually.

lessons.title: Come, Lord Jesus
lessons.hear:
A year ago, we began with a picture: the church is the body of Christ, and I am not a spectator sitting in church but an indispensable member. Today, let’s look back on the journey.

First we changed our mindset: the church is the body of Christ, the household of God, the temple of the Holy Spirit, and the bride of Christ—I don’t just go to church; I am the church. Then we changed our life: moving from self-centered to selfless, learning humility and returning to our proper place, letting the Holy Spirit grow the nine-fold fruit. Then we changed our living: worship, giving, and prayer became everyday disciplines. Next we changed our relationships: walking with our pastors, loving one another, and reconciling in conflict. Finally we changed our ministry: discovering our gifts, walking the Way of Service, bearing fruit through 920 and 235, and reaching outward to the ends of the earth. Mindset, life, living, relationships, ministry—all of it is the work of the Holy Spirit within us.

The last page of the Bible is both an invitation and a hope: “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’ He who hears, let him say, ‘Come!’” (Revelation 22:17). Like a bride, the church invites the thirsty to come and drink the water of life, even as she looks up for the Bridegroom’s return. The Lord says, “Yes, I come quickly.” And the church answers, “Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20).

On that day, people from every nation, tribe, people, and language will stand before the throne and cry out together, “Salvation be to our God, who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10). No one will say, “I did this.” So today we say it too: for every change, every fruit, and every act of service this year, all the glory goes to Jesus.

Now you are sent. Take what you have received this year back to your home, your small group, your workplace, and your community. Walk with one person, invite one person, until the Lord returns.
lessons.light: In the eight steps of changing a mindset, the last are repetition and multiplication: this year’s course is ending, but the practice is just beginning. The three foundations, the two cores, and the one purpose come down to a single sentence: let Jesus reign, let Jesus receive all the glory, and build God’s system together with all the saints as we await the Lord’s return.
think: In Revelation 22:17-21, who is saying “Come,” and what does the Lord Jesus promise?
This year, across mindset, life, living, relationships, and ministry, what change am I most grateful for?
Carrying this commission, what is the first thing I will do in the new year, and with whom?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for everything you have done in me and in our church this year. Every change is your grace, and all the glory belongs to you. Send me back to my home, my small group, and my world, to walk with people and invite people until you come again. Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus! In Jesus’ name, amen.
lessons.do: Today, with your spiritual companion or small group, have each person name in one sentence the biggest change of this year. Then lay hands on each other or hold hands and bless one another: “May Jesus reign in you, and may all glory go to him.”
lessons.quick: All glory to Jesus; go out with his commission until the Lord returns.
text: The Spirit and the bride say, “Come!” He who hears, let him say, “Come!” He who is thirsty, let him come. He who desires, let him take the water of life freely.
I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: if anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues which are written in this book.
If anyone takes away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God will take away his part from the tree of life, and out of the holy city, which are written in this book.
He who testifies these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen! Yes, come, Lord Jesus!
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with all the saints. Amen.
